papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal information from teacher models. KD methods range from matching softened teacher logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure, and are commonly combined with complementary engineering strategies (architecture design, pretraining of compact models, quantization, and data augmentation). Empirical evidence shows distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision and language tasks while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability and augmentation, and the relative strength and role of the teacher; these choices shape practical tradeoffs in robustness, fairness, and cross-distribution generalization.

papers_seen.author: Mckee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and distributed settings KD often recovers much of a teacher's predictive performance while enabling faster inference, lower memory use, and deployment under resource or privacy constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: outcomes depend on what signals are transferred (logits, features, attention), teacher–student compatibility, availability and quality of data (including data-free or federated setups), and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Best practice treats distillation as one element of a compression pipeline that combines representation matching, architecture-aware student design, data strategies, and risk-aware training protocols.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller ones to reduce inference cost, improve deployability, or impart desirable properties (robustness, fairness, interpretability). Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, ensemble consensus, attention maps) and in what data is available (original training data, synthetic data, or no data). Practical systems combine KD with architecture-level compression (pruning, structured sparsity) and with training-time strategies (online or continual distillation, curriculum schedules) to trade off efficiency and accuracy. While KD yields strong empirical results across NLP, speech, vision, and generative models, open challenges remain in data-free settings, cross-domain generalization, preserving fairness and interpretability, and designing distillation objectives that best capture the teacher’s knowledge for a given task.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Findings, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring useful predictive behavior or internal structure from one or more teachers. A rich set of KD approaches exists — from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate representation imitation, attention and feature alignment, adversarial and projector-based techniques, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or federated variants — and these have been applied across NLP, vision, graph-structured data, multimodal models, and generative models. Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher/student compatibility, data availability, and task-specific constraints. Important practical concerns include preserving rare-token behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher errors or biases, enabling privacy-preserving or data-free compression, and combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students for deployment in deep learning and NLP. A broad family of KD techniques—ranging from softened-logit supervision to intermediate representation matching, attention- and feature-level imitation, many-to-many layer alignment, adversarial and data-free variants, and task- or device-aware architecture search—enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while often retaining most of the teacher's performance. Effective application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, whether and how to use original data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. Important open problems remain regarding theoretical understanding, robustness under distribution shift or imperfect teachers, and scalable private or data-free distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, Practical Guidance, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A range of mechanisms—soft-target matching, feature and attention imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and self- or multi-teacher schemes—enable compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and energy. Practical pipelines combine KD with architecture-aware design, pretraining or warming strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization) to meet deployment constraints. However, distillation success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and the choice of distilled signals; important open problems include robust cross-domain transfer, distillation without original data, preserving rare-token or fine-grained behaviors in language tasks, and avoiding transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Targeted Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable strategy for producing compact, deployable models by transferring behavior from larger teacher models into smaller students. The field has evolved beyond matching softened output logits to include representation-level guidance, attention and relational targets, data-augmentation and synthesis strategies, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision and language shows that appropriately designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance while reducing compute, memory, and latency; however, success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability and provenance, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as one component of a compression toolkit, integrating architecture choices, precision reductions, and data strategies to meet production constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cobb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD transfers information beyond hard labels — including softened output distributions, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational signals — and is commonly combined with architectural or numerical compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest performance loss when teacher–student design, data availability, and optimization dynamics are considered; however, its success is contingent on capacity alignment, data choices, and safeguards against transferring undesirable behaviors. Applications range from accelerated inference and edge deployment to domain adaptation, federated learning, and task-specific adaptations such as non-autoregressive translation and graph-to-MLP compression.

papers_seen.author: Atkinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably yields compact models that retain much of a larger teacher’s performance when applied with attention to what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, and data availability. KD works through multiple mechanisms—soft-target regularization, representation transfer, and ensemble-derived ‘‘dark knowledge’’—and its strengths are maximized when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and task-aware training curricula. However, KD is not a universal solution: practical deployments must address limits including distribution shift, rare-token behavior, privacy-sensitive or data-free scenarios, and potential transfer of undesirable teacher behavior. I therefore argue that KD should be treated as the practical core of hybrid compression pipelines, selected and tuned according to deployment constraints and supplemented with methods that mitigate its known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large deep models into compact ones that are suitable for deployment. Across NLP, speech, vision-language, and specialized tasks such as machine reading comprehension, KD enables students to inherit performance-critical behaviors from larger teachers while enabling orders-of-magnitude reductions in model size and compute. When combined with complementary techniques (e.g., architecture search or structured pruning) and when tailored to task or domain specifics, distillation yields compressed models that approach teacher performance while meeting resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to emulate larger teacher models so that inference cost, memory, and latency are reduced while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a diverse toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and channel-wise transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schedules, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. KD is most effective when matched to student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints and is typically combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) to meet practical requirements. Important limits remain — including sensitivity to teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, robustness and fairness concerns, and data scarcity — motivating hybrid methods and careful evaluation in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students that preserve most of the teacher’s capability. When treated as a toolkit rather than a single loss function, KD supports multiple forms of transferred knowledge (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention and relational signals), and it interoperates with complementary compression methods (architecture search, pruning, quantization) and data strategies (data-free synthesis, synthetic/distilled training sets). However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability and quality, and explicit choices about what to transfer and how to align representations. Practitioners should therefore adopt KD as a first-line method while designing task- and deployment-aware distillation pipelines and monitoring known failure modes such as teacher error propagation, low-frequency token degradation, and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-line, Context-aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with attention to what knowledge is transferred, how intermediate layers are aligned, and whether data or privacy constraints hold, KD can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance while enabling large gains in inference speed and memory. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: optimization difficulties, mismatches in capacity between teacher and student, and limited or private data require tailored objectives, architecture-aware choices, and complementary techniques. This essay argues KD should be a primary strategy in model-compression toolkits while recommending concrete practices to increase reliability across real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single teacher→student soft-label transfer into a broad toolkit for compressing and adapting deep models across vision, language, and multimodal domains. Contemporary approaches extend logits matching to representation- and structure-aware objectives, multi- and continual-teaching schemes, task-aware layer selection, and combinations with pruning or architecture-level compression. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain-shift constraints but its success depends on design choices about what is transferred, how the student is supervised, data availability, and student capacity. Practical progress emphasizes representation matching beyond logits, careful layer- and channel-level alignment, and composing KD with other compression techniques; remaining challenges include robustness under distribution shift, data-free scenarios, and preserving fine-grained or safety-critical behavior.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from larger or more informative models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relations. Across vision and language tasks, KD variants (soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, self-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and projector- or channel-aware alignment) have been shown to recover much of the teacher’s performance while enabling lower-latency and lower-memory deployment. Practical success depends on choosing what to transfer, tailoring objectives to the student architecture and target task, and addressing data availability and teacher imperfections. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, representative methods, empirical patterns, and open challenges for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Beard
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of methods for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller student models so that compact systems retain much of the teachers' performance while meeting deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy). KD methods cover matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations and attention, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware variants (including data-free and few-shot approaches). In practice KD is usually combined with architecture-aware choices (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful data or synthetic-data strategies. While KD often yields strong empirical gains, its effectiveness depends on teacher–student alignment, the chosen distillation signals, and data provenance; persistent challenges include robustness to distribution shift, preserving low-frequency behaviors, and avoiding transfer of undesirable biases. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, empirical patterns, practical recommendations, and open problems for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Multi-purpose Strategy for Model Compression and Robust Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD supports domain adaptation, latency-aware architecture transformations, robustness transfer, and interpretable model surrogates. When combined with careful training protocols (e.g., multi-teacher schemes, domain adaptation, or targeted regularization), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models in resource- and latency-constrained or safety-critical settings across vision, speech, 3D perception, and natural language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing compact, efficient deep models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students. Across domains — vision, generation, control, and natural language tasks — KD enables large portions of teacher performance to be retained while enabling dramatic reductions in inference cost, memory footprint, and power consumption. When used thoughtfully (choice of distillation signal, teacher–student compatibility, and data strategy), KD integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and privacy- or data-constrained workflows to produce production-ready compact models. Equally important are mitigations for risks such as bias transfer, degraded robustness under domain shift, and failures when original training data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Efficient Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a foundational technique for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy of larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and graph domains. When applied thoughtfully — combining representational objectives, teacher-student co-design, task-aware compression, and appropriate data strategies — KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices while maintaining robustness and fairness. However, pitfalls arise from mismatches in inputs, teacher strength, data availability, and dataset biases; practical KD should therefore be integrated with complementary methods (e.g., architecture search, pruning, curriculum strategies, and data-generation) and with safeguards for ethical concerns.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted strategy for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD has been adapted into a family of techniques that vary by what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational signals), how transfer is scheduled (offline, online, multi-teacher), and how data constraints are handled (real-data, augmented, synthesized, or data-free). In practice, KD is most effective when treated as a system-level design primitive and combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, student-aware architecture design) and data strategies, but its success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful attention to robustness, fairness, and distributional generalization.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. KD enables deploying compact models that retain much of teacher performance, supports cross-modal and task-specific transfers, and can be adapted to privacy- and data-constrained settings. While highly effective in practice, KD’s outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and objective design; realizing its full potential requires targeted methodological choices such as feature-level matching, multi-teacher fusion, adversarial data synthesis, and privacy-preserving mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Gross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD operates at multiple levels (softened output distributions, intermediate features and attention maps, relational/contrastive objectives, and module-level behavior), and is commonly combined with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (data-free synthesis, public transfer sets, augmentation). Empirical work shows well-designed KD pipelines often produce compact models that approach teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and careful choice of distillation signals. Open problems include aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or domain-specific behaviors, ensuring robustness under distribution shift, and developing principled teacher design and data-limited protocols.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable route to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their predictive capability. KD achieves favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across modalities and tasks, but its real-world success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and explicit handling of robustness, fairness, and deployment constraints. A pragmatic approach treats KD as a core tool that should routinely be combined with complementary compression, data, and training strategies.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a single compression trick but a flexible set of techniques that can reduce model size, preserve or transfer task-relevant information, enable deployment in latency- and memory-constrained settings, support domain adaptation and privacy-preserving federated workflows, and be combined with structural compression. When applied thoughtfully — with task-aware selection of distilled signals, architecturally informed teacher-student design, and attention to data availability and optimization dynamics — KD yields large practical benefits for deep learning and NLP systems while avoiding common failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and pragmatic approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD can transfer predictive behavior and internal representations, and—when co-designed with architecture choices, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques—routinely yields compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability and provenance, token- or class-level coverage in the teacher, and careful handling of optimization dynamics and robustness. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, system-level tool for model compression in deep learning and NLP, used together with targeted engineering and auditing to manage its limits and to maximize practical benefit.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller students that are deployable under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, relational signals), aligning teacher and student architectures and tokenization, and combining KD with complementary techniques such as architecture search or targeted pruning—distillation routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance and sometimes even improve generalization. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on data availability, teacher quality and friendliness, domain shifts, and the specific form of knowledge chosen for transfer. Effective deployment therefore requires principled design of the distillation objective, curricula or annealing schedules, and safeguards for robustness and rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Dodson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of distillation objectives—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention- and channel-guided losses, relational/contrastive signals, and self- or multi-teacher regimes—can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to trade accuracy for latency, memory, and power. Practical success depends on aligning teacher signals to student capacity, access to (or synthesis of) suitable training data, and mitigation of optimization, fairness, and robustness risks. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, representative methods, practical recommendations, and open challenges for applying distillation in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Barker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line but Contextual Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD provides multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals) and training regimes (offline teacher-to-student, online/self-distillation, ensemble-to-single), and it can be combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints. However, KD’s success depends on careful teacher–student co-design, the choice of what knowledge to transfer, data availability or synthesis, and safeguards for robustness and privacy. Treated as a core element of a compression pipeline rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all remedy, KD yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs for many real-world applications while leaving important open problems in data-free distillation, rare-behavior preservation, and distributional robustness.

papers_seen.author: Andrews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals—and are often combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design). Across vision and language tasks, distillation commonly yields large efficiency gains with modest performance loss when teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and evaluation under realistic deployment constraints are addressed. Important ongoing challenges include data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, robustness and fairness under compression, preserving rare-token behaviors in NLP, and principled choices about which signals to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compress large neural models for deployment, while preserving performance and enabling new capabilities such as efficient federated learning, data-free compression, interpretability, and few-shot adaptation. Across architectures and tasks, KD variants—ranging from layer-to-layer alignment and progressive module replacement to meta-learned teachers and adversarial data synthesis—provide methods to trade computation, memory, and communication for small changes in accuracy. These methods make it possible to bring large pretrained models into production and edge settings, and to reconcile competing requirements such as privacy, heterogeneity, and interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Atkinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a broadly useful, pragmatic approach for shrinking large models into deployable students across vision, speech, and language tasks. Treated as a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD encompasses soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware or data-free variants. When combined with complementary structural compression (pruning, quantization) and student-aware curricula, KD frequently achieves large reductions in memory and latency while retaining most of teacher performance. However, realizing these gains in production requires careful attention to what is transferred, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit evaluation of robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have diversified from the original logits-based teacher→student paradigm into a broad set of methods that operate on features, modules, data, and training procedures. Contemporary work shows multiple complementary mechanisms for transferring knowledge—soft targets, feature- and attention-level mimicry, adversarial alignment, module replacement, and data- or communication-constrained distillation—each suited to different deployment constraints (privacy, compute, bandwidth) and model families (transformers, CNNs, GANs, GNNs). Advances emphasize (1) understanding why KD helps (stability, richer concept learning), (2) designing where to transfer knowledge (penultimate features, attention maps, projectors), and (3) tailoring the distillation process to practical settings (online multi-model training, federated environments, data-free scenarios, and teacher models optimized for students). Empirical results across vision, speech, language, generation, and retrieval indicate KD can yield compact models that retain most teacher performance when the distillation objective, the representation level, and the training dynamics are appropriately matched to the target constraints.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches to Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teachers to compact students. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed diverse strategies—teacher–student logits matching, layer-wise representation matching, adversarial sample generation, progressive module replacement, many-to-many layer mapping, and task-aware filtering—to address capacity gaps, data access limits, privacy constraints, and robustness needs. Practical deployments additionally combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, and federated protocols to meet hardware and communication budgets. Empirical work shows that careful design of distillation objectives and inputs can preserve most of the teacher’s accuracy and even transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, while specialized schemes enable distillation without original training data or across continual/heterogeneous settings.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of the teacher's performance. KD succeeds when its objectives, representation targets, and training regimes are chosen to match deployment constraints and student capacity; combining KD with complementary techniques (architecture search, pruning, data-free synthesis, and online protocols) extends its reach. However, KD also transfers risks (bias, privacy leakage, fragility) and faces limits when teacher signals are mismatched or training data are scarce, motivating task-aware design, robust distillation objectives, and emergent meta- and data-free methods.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applicable strategy for compressing large neural models by transferring information from one or more high-capacity teacher models to smaller student models. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals), how teacher and student are aligned, and the data available for training, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of the original performance. KD also integrates naturally with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adapts to specialized settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, heterogeneous-device deployments, generative-model compression, low-precision inference, and privacy-sensitive or data-limited environments. However, KD is not uniformly automatic: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, student capacity, distributional match, and design of distillation objectives and curricula.

papers_seen.author: Carter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression: Effectiveness, Limits, and Practical Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. When treated as a system—choosing which signals to transfer (logits, features, attention), aligning teacher and student architectures, managing data and sample selection, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques—KD yields strong accuracy/efficiency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks. Its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and attention to robustness and rare-token behavior; hence KD is best used as the central element of a broader compression pipeline rather than as a standalone fix.

papers_seen.author: French
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks KD has matured into a flexible toolkit—spanning softened-logit transfer, intermediate-representation and attention matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware or data-free variants—that, when combined with architecture-aware design and other compression primitives (pruning, quantization), enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while retaining much of a teacher's predictive power. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, availability and provenance of data, and evaluation of robustness, fairness, and distributional generalization. Ongoing challenges include reliable distillation under data scarcity or domain shift, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors in NLP, and avoiding transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Bender
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression: Capabilities, Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded toolkit that enables compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. By transferring richer supervision than hard labels—ranging from softened outputs to intermediate representations and relational signals—KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when paired with architecture-aware design and complementary compression methods. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent: success requires matching distilled signals to student capacity, careful teacher–student co-design, data strategies (including synthetic or data-free approaches), and explicit attention to robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy concerns. Treating KD as the backbone of an integrated compression pipeline delivers the best practical outcomes while acknowledging and mitigating its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied deliberately — choosing what to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity, and handling data- and deployment-specific constraints — KD yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, distillation is not automatic: outcomes depend on teacher strength and training, student architecture and capacity, the form of distilled signals, data availability (including data‑free settings), and fairness/privacy goals. Best practice treats KD as a core component combined with architecture-aware design, data strategies, and deployment-aware procedures to produce reliable, efficient models for real applications.

papers_seen.author: Hayes
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When used as a system-level strategy—choosing appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student capacities, and combining KD with complementary compression methods—KD routinely delivers favorable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and memory in vision and language tasks. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: data availability, teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift, and robustness or fairness concerns limit what a distilled student can inherit reliably. Effective deployment therefore treats KD as the default first-line method within a broader compression pipeline that includes architecture-aware design, data strategies (including data-free or privacy-aware approaches), and explicit evaluation for rare or out-of-distribution behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical, Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic family of techniques for turning large, high‑performing models into smaller, deployable ones. When treated as a system‑level design choice rather than a single loss term, KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and inference cost while often preserving much of a teacher's predictive power. Realizing these benefits in practice requires choosing what knowledge to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacities, and combining KD with complementary practices such as compact pre‑training, data augmentation, or privacy‑aware data synthesis. KD is powerful but not universal: its effectiveness depends on data availability, teacher quality, and deployment constraints, so practitioners must evaluate and adapt distillation strategies to their task and context.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger, high-capacity models to smaller, efficient models to reduce inference cost and memory while preserving performance. Approaches span soft-label (logit) matching, feature- or attention-level imitation, multi-teacher fusion, data-free distillation, and adaptations for domain shift and heterogeneous deployment. Empirical results show distilled students can approach or match teacher performance in many settings, but success depends on teacher quality, the form of transferred knowledge, training curricula, and application-specific design choices. Emerging theoretical and empirical analyses clarify when and why distillation helps and reveal practical tradeoffs such as bias–variance effects of soft labels and the roles of ensemble and self-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Context-Dependent Path to Compact NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. When combined with complementary strategies—appropriate pretraining, architecture-aware compression, data management, or teacher-free alternatives—KD can produce compact models that retain much of the performance of large teachers. However, KD is not a universal remedy: success depends on what is distilled, how student and teacher are matched, the availability and provenance of data, and the need to manage transferred biases, robustness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques that transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving performance. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals), how data are used or synthesized, and how training is scheduled (offline, online, self-distillation, adversarial compression). Empirical work shows KD can enable deployable models across vision, speech, and NLP, but success depends on aligning teacher-student inputs and representations, addressing optimization mismatches, and adapting objectives to task and data constraints. Open challenges include data-free distillation, cross-domain generalization, robustness, fairness, and principled choices of distillation targets for heterogeneous student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Riggs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Dependent Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities, but its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability and provenance, and robustness or fairness objectives. Treating KD as a central building block—combined with architecture-aware compression, representation matching, data strategies, and task-aware curricula—produces the most reliable trade-offs for real deployments. Emerging theoretical analyses and diverse application studies show both why KD works and where it fails, motivating principled combinations of KD with complementary techniques in production systems.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Freeman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal signals so students meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. The field has evolved from soft-label matching to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-representation and attention alignment, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and data-free or adversarial sample synthesis; KD is frequently combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and domain-aware pretraining. Empirical and emerging theoretical work highlight both KD’s practical utility and its limits — success depends on teacher–student compatibility, availability and provenance of data, choice of transferred signals, and optimization curricula — motivating integrated pipelines and ongoing research on robustness, rare-token fidelity in sequence tasks, and privacy-preserving distillation.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Methods and Challenges in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across vision, generative modeling, and NLP, researchers have developed logit- and feature-level distillation, task-specific adaptations, multi-teacher schemes, and teacher-optimization strategies to improve student accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. Work also focuses on constraints arising in distributed and privacy-preserving settings, on preserving rare or fine-grained information, and on adapting distillation to complex tasks such as detection, generation, and dense prediction. Practical systems combine architectural choices, training curricula, and distilled supervision to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for deployment.
