papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Theory, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely used approach to compressing large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. KD methods span soft-logit matching, ensemble distillation, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, self- and multi-teacher schedules, and privacy- or data-aware variants. Empirical results across vision and language tasks show that carefully chosen distillation targets and student–teacher alignment can achieve large reductions in inference cost with modest loss (and sometimes gains) in performance. However, practical success depends on capacity-matching, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of failure modes such as propagation of teacher errors, degraded rare-token behavior in NLP, and privacy concerns. KD performs best as a component of a broader compression pipeline that includes architecture choices, pruning/quantization, and data-centric strategies.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models so that students retain much of the teachers' task performance while reducing inference cost and resource consumption. The practice extends beyond matching final logits to include feature- and layer-level supervision, attention- or projector-based alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware strategies (including data-free or synthetic-data approaches). KD has been applied across modalities and deployment regimes (on-device, privacy-aware, and distributed/federated settings), and empirical work highlights both practical successes and recurring failure modes such as sensitivity to teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, and preservation of rare or low-frequency signals. Current best practices emphasize combining representation-level objectives, careful input/data handling, and co-design of teacher and student; open problems remain around robustness, heterogeneity, and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students that preserve most of the teacher’s capability. When treated as a toolkit rather than a single loss function, KD supports multiple forms of transferred knowledge (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention and relational signals), and it interoperates with complementary compression methods (architecture search, pruning, quantization) and data strategies (data-free synthesis, synthetic/distilled training sets). However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability and quality, and explicit choices about what to transfer and how to align representations. Practitioners should therefore adopt KD as a first-line method while designing task- and deployment-aware distillation pipelines and monitoring known failure modes such as teacher error propagation, low-frequency token degradation, and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression techniques have become central to deploying deep models under computation, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. Over the past decade researchers have developed a spectrum of KD methods — teacher→student transfer, feature-level and adversarial distillation, data-free (zero-shot) distillation, online/multi-teacher schemes, and combinations of KD with pruning and architecture search — and applied them across domains including vision, multimodal models, graph and medical data, and NLP. Empirical results repeatedly show that appropriately designed distillation can produce much smaller, faster, or more private models with modest loss (or sometimes gain) in accuracy, while remaining sensitive to dataset availability, domain shift, and adversarial robustness. Current best practices emphasize matching representations beyond logits, designing student-friendly supervision, and combining KD with structural compression; remaining challenges include KD under data heterogeneity or privacy constraints, transferring robustness, and automating student architectures for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Vaughan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Capabilities, Constraints, and Best‑Practice Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted toolkit for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. Treated as a pipeline rather than a single loss term, KD spans soft-target supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, multi-teacher or online schedules, and data-aware or data-free protocols. When co-designed with student architectures and combined with complementary structural compression (pruning, quantization) and data strategies, KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, reliable deployment demands explicit attention to teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability (few-shot or zero-shot regimes), preservation of rare or safety-critical behaviors, and mitigation of transferred biases and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Hayes
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When used as a system-level strategy—choosing appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student capacities, and combining KD with complementary compression methods—KD routinely delivers favorable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and memory in vision and language tasks. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: data availability, teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift, and robustness or fairness concerns limit what a distilled student can inherit reliably. Effective deployment therefore treats KD as the default first-line method within a broader compression pipeline that includes architecture-aware design, data strategies (including data-free or privacy-aware approaches), and explicit evaluation for rare or out-of-distribution behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under memory, latency, or privacy constraints. The literature has converged on a set of recurring methods (soft-target/logit supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, multi-teacher schedules, data-free and privacy-aware protocols) and deployment practices (combining KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search). Empirical evidence demonstrates that appropriately designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional alignment. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors (especially in NLP), and principled teacher–student co-design and curricula for difficult tasks.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Path to Compact, High-Quality Models in NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models for deployment. Across NLP and other modalities, distillation enables lightweight architectures to retain much of a teacher's performance while supporting additional compression techniques (pruning, quantization) and privacy-respecting or data-free workflows. However, distillation outcomes depend strongly on teacher–student compatibility, the form of distilled knowledge (logits, features, attention), access to data, and optimization choices. Best results arise when distillation is integrated with appropriate pre-training, architectural adapters (projectors or attention alignment), and, when necessary, data synthesis or domain adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Castaneda
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Patterns, and Practical Caveats
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile toolkit that transfers richer supervision from larger or heterogeneous teacher models into smaller students to reduce inference cost while retaining task performance. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals), composes with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design), and can be adapted to domain-specific settings (generative models, recommenders, distributed training). Its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data alignment, choice of signals to transfer, and mitigation strategies for robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy. When applied with principled design—matching distilled signals to student capacity, using teacher-aware curricula, and combining with other compression tools—KD frequently yields production-ready efficiency gains, but it is not a universal remedy and requires careful engineering to avoid failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Concise Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of teacher performance. Research across vision, speech, translation, and NLP tasks has developed multiple KD objectives (soft logits, intermediate-feature matching, attention or projector-based alignment), training regimes (offline teacher–student, self-distillation, multi-teacher, adversarial transfer), and data strategies (data-free, distilled datasets, and hybrid authentic/synthetic training). Empirical and theoretical work explains why KD often improves student generalization (dark-knowledge regularization, transferred inductive biases) while also documenting limitations (capacity mismatch, teacher error propagation, distributional/low-frequency failures) and practical remedies. Best practice is to treat KD as a flexible toolkit and combine it with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. When combined with representation-level objectives, architecture-aware techniques, and deployment-aware protocols, KD preserves much of teacher performance while enabling real-world constraints such as latency, memory, and device heterogeneity to be met. Best practices include selecting appropriate distilled signals (beyond soft labels), pretraining or warming students, and aligning objectives with deployment constraints. Despite strong empirical success across modalities, open challenges remain in handling data heterogeneity, domain shift, privacy-sensitive settings, and the automated design of student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compress large models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. KD techniques that move beyond naive logit matching — for example by mimicking intermediate features, adapting teacher-student interactions to the task, or training teachers that are optimized for transfer — yield larger gains in both vision and language settings. KD also enables new training regimes (online and distributed) and can be combined with architecture search to produce task-aware compressed models. At the same time, interactions between KD and other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing) and the choice of what and how to transfer require careful design. Overall, KD is a mature and expanding toolkit that, when applied with methodical choices about knowledge type, teacher strategy, and training setup, provides an effective path to deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques constitute a flexible toolkit for converting large, high-performing deep models into smaller, deployable students. Across speech, vision, and natural language tasks, practitioners transfer predictive behavior and selected internal structure from teachers to students to reduce latency, memory, and energy while preserving task performance. The literature shows a spectrum of methods (soft-targets, representation matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free approaches), trade-offs that depend on student capacity and data access, and practical strategies that pair distillation with pretraining, architecture design, and data interventions. Important limitations remain around domain shift, rare-token or low-frequency behavior, theoretical characterization of what transfers, and privacy-aware or data-free distillation regimes.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. KD methods include soft-output (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational or contrastive objectives, and more recent data-free, multi-teacher, and online/self-distillation variants. When combined with architecture-aware transformations such as pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search, KD enables practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and memory that are critical for deploying NLP systems. Remaining challenges include distillation without original data, preserving rare-token and fine-grained behaviors, robustness under distribution shift and adversarial settings, and safeguarding fairness and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, efficient students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. A broad family of KD techniques has been developed—matching softened logits, aligning intermediate representations or attention, using multi-teacher or online co-training schedules, and synthesizing or augmenting data for training students. KD often recovers much of a teacher's performance while reducing parameter count and inference cost, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data alignment, and training dynamics. Practical deployments combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, progressive module replacement) and must address open challenges including heterogeneous or federated settings, data scarcity or privacy constraints, robustness under distribution shift, and preservation of low-frequency or domain-specific signals.

papers_seen.author: Barton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. It consistently enables substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while often preserving much of teacher performance when applied with attention to signals transferred, student capacity, data alignment, and complementary compression techniques. KD should therefore be treated as a core component of practical compression pipelines, but its success requires matching methods to task and deployment constraints and explicit handling of known failure modes such as domain shift, rare-token degradation, and potential propagation of teacher errors.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, broadly applicable family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their predictive power. KD enables large gains in inference speed, reduced memory footprint, and practical deployment under latency, compute, and privacy constraints. However, straightforward distillation can transfer undesirable properties and can underperform when data is limited or teacher–student mismatches are large. To realize KD's full potential practitioners should combine soft-target transfer with representation matching, targeted data augmentation or data-free synthesis, careful teacher design (including ensembles or student-aware teachers), and explicit robustness or privacy-aware objectives. These combined practices produce compact models that are accurate, efficient, and more robust for real-world NLP and deep-learning deployments.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single logit-matching trick into a versatile, task- and deployment-aware toolkit that can produce compact models with strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. By transferring soft targets, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals, and by integrating with architecture search, data augmentation, and heterogeneous-teacher setups, KD enables practical compression across vision and language modalities. This paper argues KD should be a first-line technique for model compression in deep learning and NLP, describes the complementary methods that make it effective in production settings, and highlights common pitfalls and practical remedies for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers in both vision and natural language tasks. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints, and many variants extend KD beyond soft-target transfer to feature matching, multi-teacher schemes, progressive replacement, and domain-adaptive workflows. At the same time, theoretical and empirical analyses reveal optimization barriers, sensitivity to the choice of data and teacher signals, and imperfect matching between teacher and student as important limits. This review argues that KD is a powerful but context-dependent tool: its success requires matching the distillation signal to student capacity and task complexity, combining KD with complementary compression techniques, and paying careful attention to data and training dynamics to avoid degenerate outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Brewer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high‑performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. The field has developed a broad toolkit—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations and attention, relational and feature-level transfer, multi‑teacher and online schemes, and data‑free variants—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss when teacher–student design, data strategies, and optimization choices are carefully managed. Remaining challenges include principled selection of distilled signals, handling teacher–student mismatch, preserving robustness and fairness under compression, and operating under limited or no access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable smaller, faster models to inherit performance characteristics from larger models. Research has introduced multiple KD paradigms—teacher-student soft-label transfer, self-distillation, feature/internal-representation matching, multi-teacher strategies, and data-augmentation–aware distillation—each addressing different practical constraints such as domain shift, resource limits, or heterogeneous architectures. Applications span speech, machine translation evaluation, ASR, and domain-specific pretrained models; empirical work shows substantial reductions in model size and latency can be achieved with modest accuracy loss, or sometimes even gains, when distillation is combined with architectural adaptations and training-time strategies. Remaining challenges include transferring internal representations across heterogeneous architectures, choosing or designing teachers that are most useful for particular students, and preserving low-frequency or domain-specific signals during aggressive compression.

papers_seen.author: Chandler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible, deployable pathway to shrink large models while retaining most of their predictive power. When treated as a central design primitive and combined with representation-level objectives, data strategies, and architecture-aware choices, KD enables substantial gains in latency, memory, and deployability across tasks from classification and sequence generation to detection and lifelong learning. However, reliable deployment requires careful attention to teacher–student alignment, data availability and augmentation, and task-specific adaptations.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, KD has evolved from simple logit matching to a diverse toolkit that includes intermediate-feature imitation, multi-teacher fusion, data- and communication-constrained protocols, and progressive module replacement. Empirical work shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while substantially reducing memory, compute, and latency, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student alignment, and training protocols. Important open issues include robust transfer under distribution shift, efficient distillation when teacher cost is high, and preserving fairness and safety properties in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Andrews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals—and are often combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design). Across vision and language tasks, distillation commonly yields large efficiency gains with modest performance loss when teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and evaluation under realistic deployment constraints are addressed. Important ongoing challenges include data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, robustness and fairness under compression, preserving rare-token behaviors in NLP, and principled choices about which signals to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of methods that transfers richer supervision from large teacher models to compact students in order to reduce inference cost while retaining predictive performance. KD covers logit/soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, channel- and feature-level transfers, self- and online-distillation, and multi-teacher and data-free variants. Its effectiveness depends on alignment between teacher and student capacity, the choice of what to transfer, data availability, and deployment constraints; therefore KD should be treated as a central component of modern compression pipelines but always applied with task- and context-aware adaptations and complementary compression primitives.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD encompasses logit-level soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational or ensemble signals, and many practical variants (online, self-distillation, data-free). When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student co-design, KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for classification, sequence tasks, retrieval, and generative systems. However, KD is not universally effective: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and distributional match, and the choice of distillation signals; open problems include reliable distillation without original data, preserving low-frequency or rare behaviors in NLP, and avoiding transfer of undesirable properties such as biases or fragility.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to emulate larger teacher models so that inference cost, memory, and latency are reduced while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a diverse toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and channel-wise transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schedules, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. KD is most effective when matched to student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints and is typically combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) to meet practical requirements. Important limits remain — including sensitivity to teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, robustness and fairness concerns, and data scarcity — motivating hybrid methods and careful evaluation in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks, KD variants — including soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, self-distillation, and progressive module replacement — have been shown to reduce inference cost and memory while retaining much of the teacher's utility. Practical deployments combine KD with complementary techniques (data augmentation, low-precision numerics, teacher adaptation, and data-filtering) and must manage failure modes stemming from teacher–student capacity mismatch, data availability, and domain shift. The field continues to refine what knowledge to transfer, how to perform transfer efficiently, and how to preserve robustness and privacy in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Stephens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, System-Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact models that retain much of larger models' performance. Treated as a system-level strategy rather than a single loss term, KD yields deployable students by transferring soft outputs and internal representations and by composing naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies. Its effectiveness depends on careful teacher–student alignment, selection of distilled signals, and attention to data regimes and robustness concerns. When applied with task-aware design and complementary compression techniques, KD delivers strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for real-world deep learning and NLP deployments.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a core tool for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Evidence across vision, multimodal, and NLP tasks shows distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling quantization, faster inference, and privacy-aware deployment. However, distillation is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, data unavailability, modality mismatches, and safety/robustness concerns can limit how closely a student can match its teacher. Combining complementary techniques—feature-level mimicry, intermediate-attention alignment, multi-teacher schedules, confidence-weighted losses, and generative or data-free strategies—yields the most reliable compressed models in practice.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First-Line, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and empirically validated approach for converting large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Treated as a toolkit rather than a single loss, KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), training regimes (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free), and integration with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design). I argue KD should serve as the first-line strategy for model compression in modern deep learning and NLP pipelines, provided practitioners adopt principled, context-aware distillation recipes and pair KD with targeted validation for robustness and distributional concerns.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) into smaller, cheaper models (students) by using richer supervision than hard labels alone. The literature has developed multiple complementary strategies—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, architecturally guided replacement, multi-teacher schedules, data- and privacy-aware variants, and teacher-training schemes—to address deployment constraints, domain shift, and limited or private data. Empirical work shows these approaches can close much of the performance gap to full-size models across classification, language understanding, and retrieval tasks; theoretical and empirical analyses explain why distillation often improves generalization beyond mere compression. Remaining challenges include input distribution mismatch, low-frequency token fidelity in sequence tasks, and robust distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Ferguson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically supported approach for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a design paradigm rather than a single loss term, KD yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks, interoperates with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), and supports variants for heterogeneous or low-data deployments. However, KD is not automatic: its success depends on student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data availability, and defenses against teacher errors, distribution shift, and privacy leakage. I argue KD should be the default first-line method for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP, applied with principled teacher–student design and targeted mitigations for known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Burke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical and flexible pathway to convert large, high‑performing models into compact students suitable for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When matched to student capacity and task constraints, distillation can preserve most of a teacher’s performance while enabling complementary compression (quantization, pruning) and deployment strategies. Realistic application of KD requires attention to what signals are transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention, or relational structure), how teacher and student inputs and architectures are aligned, and how limited or synthetic data are used. KD also carries risks—propagation of teacher errors, loss of rare‑token behavior, domain shift sensitivity, and privacy issues—that mandate task‑aware design and evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Current Understandings of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used model compression paradigm in which a smaller student model is trained to capture the behavior of a larger teacher model. It has been applied across domains (vision, NLP, recommender systems, medical imaging) to reduce model size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Work in the field explores what is transferred (soft outputs, internal representations, feature relations), how to improve transfer (adversarial samples, contrastive objectives, structural transformations), and how to address practical constraints (absence of original data, domain shift, privacy, fairness and robustness). Empirical results show KD often yields substantial memory and runtime benefits with modest accuracy loss and can be combined with pruning, quantization and architecture search. Yet KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, imperfect teacher signals, and mismatches between teacher and student capacity can limit how closely a student matches a teacher; research continues into theoretical explanations and robust, data-efficient methods.

papers_seen.author: Singh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression: Capabilities, Limits, and a Pragmatic Integration Strategy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically grounded approach for converting large neural teachers into smaller, deployable students. Treated as a multi-signal toolbox rather than a single loss, KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and power while preserving much of teacher performance. However, distillation is not a universal cure: its success depends on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability and provenance, and targeted remedies for robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy. A practical stance treats KD as the central element of a hybrid compression pipeline that deliberately combines representation-aware objectives, architecture-aware choices, and data-aware or privacy-preserving workflows to realize reliable, efficient models for real-world NLP and deep-learning deployments.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, expressive models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple logit-matching to a diverse toolkit that includes feature- and layer-level supervision, multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, self-distillation and teacher optimization, and approaches that enable data-free or privacy-preserving compression. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling faster inference and smaller footprints; however, practical success depends on choices about objectives, alignment between teacher and student, data availability, and robustness to domain shift. Open directions include stronger theoretical characterization of what is transferred, principled treatment of heterogeneous teachers, and tighter integration of KD with quantization, pruning, and privacy mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression are indispensable tools to deploy high-performing deep models under compute, memory, privacy, and latency constraints. Across modalities and tasks, effective compression requires more than copying teacher logits: practitioners should match richer internal representations, align inputs and tokenization across teacher and student, design teacher updates that explicitly optimize transfer, and account for privacy and robustness needs. When applied thoughtfully, KD can produce compact models that retain much of the teacher’s utility and in some cases improve efficiency beyond the original models.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Evidence for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) enables deployment of high-performing but large neural models by training compact student models that mimic larger teachers. Empirical work across speech, NLP, vision, and federated settings shows KD reduces model size and inference cost while preserving accuracy, and its effectiveness increases when combined with complementary techniques: pre-training compact architectures, adaptive layer mapping for transformers, data-centric augmentations, ensemble teachers, and robustness-aware objectives. This paper synthesizes results from recent studies to argue that a principled KD pipeline—pre-train compact students, match representations flexibly, leverage data augmentation and teacher ensembles, and incorporate robustness or task-specific objectives—yields the best tradeoff between efficiency and performance for practical deployments.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers in both vision and natural language tasks. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints, and many variants extend KD beyond soft-target transfer to feature matching, multi-teacher schemes, progressive replacement, and domain-adaptive workflows. At the same time, theoretical and empirical analyses reveal optimization barriers, sensitivity to the choice of data and teacher signals, and imperfect matching between teacher and student as important limits. This review argues that KD is a powerful but context-dependent tool: its success requires matching the distillation signal to student capacity and task complexity, combining KD with complementary compression techniques, and paying careful attention to data and training dynamics to avoid degenerate outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Mcdaniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a primary, practical strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students, but it must be applied as a multi-strategy, context-aware engineering approach. When combined with representation-level objectives, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance and meet deployment constraints. However, KD is not a universal remedy: limits arise from data scarcity, teacher errors, student capacity gaps, robustness and fairness concerns, rare-token behaviors in language models, and privacy constraints. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a central tool within a broader compression toolkit and adopt targeted mitigation strategies for its known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied and practically effective set of methods for producing smaller, faster models from larger, high-capacity teachers. KD unifies a range of strategies—from matching soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations and generating synthetic training data—and is commonly combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, data and augmentation strategies, and handling of domain shift or limited-data settings. The literature identifies both methodological extensions (multi-teacher fusion, online distillation, meta-learned teachers, data-free schemes) and recurring challenges (optimization mismatch, rare-token fidelity, privacy-aware transfer) that structure ongoing research and practical guidance.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches to Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teachers to compact students. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed diverse strategies—teacher–student logits matching, layer-wise representation matching, adversarial sample generation, progressive module replacement, many-to-many layer mapping, and task-aware filtering—to address capacity gaps, data access limits, privacy constraints, and robustness needs. Practical deployments additionally combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, and federated protocols to meet hardware and communication budgets. Empirical work shows that careful design of distillation objectives and inputs can preserve most of the teacher’s accuracy and even transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, while specialized schemes enable distillation without original training data or across continual/heterogeneous settings.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: The Practical Foundations and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. Its success arises from multiple complementary mechanisms—soft-target regularization, internal representation transfer, and architectural or data-side adaptations—that together explain why KD works across modalities (vision, language, graphs) and tasks (classification, QA, generation). However, KD is not a silver bullet: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, data properties (including augmentation and low-frequency phenomena), and deployment constraints such as federated or heterogeneous environments. Recognizing these mechanisms and limitations enables principled choices (e.g., teacher design, feature/projector choices, multi-teacher or adversarial schemes, and data strategies) to get the best trade-offs between compression and performance.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Practical, but Not a Panacea
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are essential tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. A wide family of methods — from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature transfer, projector-based alignment, data-free synthesis, and combinations with pruning or architecture search — let practitioners trade compute and memory for modest accuracy loss. However, KD’s effectiveness depends on optimization, data alignment, and the choice of distilled signals; it can replicate undesirable teacher behaviors and fails when teacher–student mismatch or data constraints are not addressed. Practical deployment therefore requires selecting KD variants that match application constraints and combining distillation with complementary compression and robustness techniques.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Espinoza
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Outcomes, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal signals from teachers. Over the past decade KD has broadened from simple soft-label matching to a diverse set of techniques — intermediate-feature and attention alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, data- or generator-based synthesis, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirically, distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and training dynamics. Open problems remain in robustness to domain shift, preserving rare-token fidelity in sequence tasks, privacy- and data-constrained distillation, and principled selection of distilled signals for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Everett
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, System‑Level Strategy for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated paradigm for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. Treated as a system-level strategy—one that selects what knowledge to transfer, aligns teacher and student capacity, and composes with complementary compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies)—KD delivers strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for many practical applications. However, its success is conditional: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, distribution shift, and robustness/fairness concerns constrain outcomes, so KD must be applied thoughtfully and evaluated across deployment metrics.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become practical tools to reduce model size and computation while retaining much of the performance of large teachers. Across vision, speech, and natural language tasks, approaches include transferring soft logits, mimicking internal features or attention maps, layering/structural adaptations, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-preserving methods. Empirical results demonstrate that careful distillation can yield compact students that approach teacher accuracy and enable deployment in resource-constrained settings, but open challenges remain in robustness, task-specific distillation design, and distributed training dynamics.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Carroll
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted strategy to compress large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks, KD variants have demonstrated the ability to recover much of a teacher model’s performance while substantially reducing inference latency and memory. Practical deployments treat KD as a flexible, system-level primitive—selecting what to transfer (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), how to expose students to training data (real, synthesized, or online), and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical successes coexist with practical limits: teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, and risks of transferring undesirable behaviors or losing robustness remain active research and engineering concerns.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students that retain much of the teacher’s performance. KD spans soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, layer-aware alignment, self-distillation, and architecture-replacement strategies. When combined with appropriate pre-training, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture changes), KD enables practical tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, and memory for NLP and other modalities. Effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, what form of knowledge is transferred, and constraints such as data availability, privacy, fairness, and domain shift.
