papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Work across vision and language shows a set of recurring strategies: transfer using softened outputs (soft targets), imitation of intermediate/internal representations, layer mapping between teacher and student, task-adaptive architecture search, self-distillation, and data-free distillation when original training data are unavailable. Empirical results indicate that properly designed distillation can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while offering large gains in inference speed and memory; however, success depends on which knowledge is transferred (outputs vs. internal features), how layers are aligned, and whether task specificity and data availability are addressed. The field currently balances practical engineering (architecture and search) with algorithmic refinements (losses and training regimes), and open challenges include robust data-free methods, principled many-to-many layer matching, and teacher designs that are optimized to be “student-friendly.”

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Lin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfers information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. KD encompasses soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention or relational alignment, multi-teacher and online strategies, and task- or data-aware adaptations. Practical compression typically combines KD with architecture-aware design, pretraining, data strategies (including data-free synthesis), and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, or layer skipping). Success depends on careful matching of distilled signals to the student architecture and deployment constraints; important open problems include handling teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift and heterogeneity, preserving rare or low-frequency information, and maintaining robustness and privacy in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Haynes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, general-purpose approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. When applied with attention to what knowledge is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), to teacher–student capacity alignment, and to data constraints, KD routinely yields substantial improvements in inference latency and memory while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: it carries risks (transfer of bias, privacy leakage, reduced robustness on distribution shift and rare tokens) and requires complementary techniques (task-aware objectives, architecture design, dataset strategies, and robustness/privacy safeguards) to be reliable in production. I argue KD should be treated as the first‑line, default strategy for model compression in deep learning and NLP, used proactively alongside targeted mitigations for its limits and with careful empirical validation.

papers_seen.author: Boyd
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Research over the past decade has produced a diverse set of objectives and training regimes—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and layer-wise alignment, attention/relational signals, data- or privacy-aware synthesis, and teacher–student co-design—that together enable substantial reductions in inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, available data, teacher/student compatibility, and complementary compression techniques; open challenges include robust transfer under domain shift, distillation without original data, and principled handling of heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. The literature describes a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), training regimes (offline, online, multi‑teacher) and data strategies (original data, augmented or synthetic data, and data‑free variants). KD is frequently combined with architectural or precision changes such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and deployment constraints including privacy and robustness. Best practices treat distillation as a system-level pipeline that integrates pretraining, tailored distillation objectives, and complementary compression techniques to achieve reliable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs in real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multi-Strategy, Practical Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD can preserve much of a teacher’s predictive power while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Best results arise when distillation is combined with complementary techniques — representation matching, ensembling, architecture-aware compression, pretraining of compact students, and data-aware strategies — and when practitioners account for deployment-specific mismatches (domain shift, heterogeneous inputs, or limited access to data). Remaining challenges include robustly transferring rare or low-frequency information, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing data-free or privacy-preserving distillation that reliably generalizes under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques provide practical pathways to convert large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. Empirically, KD can transfer predictive behavior and internal representations to students that retain much of the teacher’s effectiveness, especially when combined with complementary strategies such as pre-training of compact architectures, careful layer or module mapping, and data-management methods. Successful pipelines trade off accuracy, latency, and model size while navigating constraints such as limited or private data and domain shift. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness (including rare-token behavior), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and developing principled data-free or privacy-preserving distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teachers' performance. Modern KD extends beyond soft-label matching to include representation-level objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, data-free or zero-shot variants, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search. KD has been applied successfully across domains — including language generation, ranking, detection, and federated settings — but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to manage data, privacy, and distributional shift. Practical deployment requires selecting distillation signals and training regimes that match student capacity and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Manning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Bounded Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD provides multiple mechanisms—soft-target transfer, intermediate representation matching, attention/relational signals, online and multi-teacher schedules, and data-free or synthesized-data variants—that often recover much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what and how to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and attention to robustness, fairness, and rare-token behavior. KD therefore functions best as a central component within a broader compression and deployment pipeline rather than as a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central model-compression approach that trains compact student models to emulate larger teacher models so that inference cost, memory, and deployment barriers are reduced while retaining much of the teacher’s predictive behavior. Research has produced a family of distillation objectives (soft-targets, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational losses), training regimes (offline, online, self-distillation, multi-teacher), and system-level integrations (pruning, structured sparsity, quantization, and architecture search). Empirical studies show well-designed distillation pipelines commonly recover a large fraction of teacher performance and sometimes improve generalization, but success depends on what knowledge is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical use therefore combines algorithmic choices with architecture-aware compression and data strategies tailored to the task and environment.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line, System‑Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated as a core, first‑line strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students when the method is applied as part of a system‑level pipeline. KD reliably reduces inference cost and model size while retaining much of a teacher’s performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, provided practitioners attend to what form of knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and how distillation is combined with structural compression and data strategies. KD’s strengths are its methodological flexibility (soft targets, feature and attention matching, multi‑teacher schedules, and data synthesis) and its ability to compose with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Its principal limits arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, and risks of transferring undesirable teacher behaviors; these require explicit remedies (capacity-aware student design, representation projection, multi‑teacher or synthetic data, and robustness evaluation). When deployed as an engineering pipeline rather than a single loss term, KD yields compact models that meet practical latency, memory, and deployment constraints while exposing clear research challenges around robustness, privacy, and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Principled Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical technique for compressing large neural models into deployable, efficient students while preserving much of teacher performance. Across supervised, self-supervised, multi-task, and low-precision settings, distillation can recover large-model accuracy in smaller footprints when combined with careful design choices that address capacity mismatch, task relevance, and the nature of the transferred knowledge. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on distillation schedule, selection of what to transfer (logits, features, or task-aware subsets), and occasionally on teacher improvement or specialization. Understanding these interactions is key to robust compression for production NLP and deep-learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary tools to shrink large deep models for deployment while retaining much of their predictive power. Across vision, speech and natural language processing, researchers have developed a range of approaches that operate at the level of logits (soft labels), intermediate representations, modules/layers, or training curricula, and have combined KD with complementary strategies such as architecture search, quantization, and generative replay. Empirical work shows that distilled students can often approach teacher performance while achieving large reductions in size and latency, but the effectiveness of different KD strategies depends strongly on task, data distribution, teacher strength, and practical constraints such as availability of original training data. Important challenges remain in transferring robustness, handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving rare-token behavior, and balancing bias–variance tradeoffs introduced by soft supervision.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Hunter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints. Across vision and language tasks KD methods—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature and relational alignment—consistently enable substantial reductions in compute and memory while recovering much of teacher accuracy when applied with attention to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization dynamics. Practical KD pipelines typically combine distilled signals with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adopt data-aware strategies (augmentation, synthetic-data generation, or data-free protocols) to address real-world deployment challenges. Key open problems include robustly preserving long-tail or rare behaviors, handling distribution shift and privacy constraints, and automating student design for strict resource budgets.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Failure Modes, and Practical Recipes
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, recommendation, and NLP. KD techniques range from simple logits matching to representation-level transfer, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial sample synthesis, and progressive module replacement. While many distillation recipes recover most of a teacher’s accuracy and enable large efficiency gains, the success of KD depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or absent training data. Careful design—matching distillation targets to student capacity, mitigating transferred errors, and combining distillation with complementary compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search)—yields robust, efficient models for practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multi‑Strategy, Practical — but Bounded — Path for Compressing Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision and language tasks. When applied thoughtfully — combining soft-label transfer with representation-level guidance, architecture-aware design, and data strategies — KD enables compact models that meet memory, latency, and deployment constraints while retaining most of a teacher’s performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy: limited or private data, teacher errors, student capacity gaps, and robustness or fairness concerns create concrete failure modes that require complementary methods and careful evaluation. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a multi-strategy engineering approach whose best results arise from combining several targeted techniques that suit task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Juarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students suitable for deployment under compute, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. Across vision and NLP, KD methods extend beyond logit matching to include intermediate-representation imitation, attention and relational losses, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-constrained or data-free procedures. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation pipelines—especially when combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, or quantization—regularly yield compact models that recover much of the teacher’s performance, though open challenges remain around robustness, domain shift, fairness, and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Beyond Dark Knowledge: A Practical Position on How and Why Knowledge Distillation Works for Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile toolkit for compressing large models and adapting knowledge across architectures, domains, and devices. Its effectiveness derives from multiple mechanisms: soft-target regularization that shapes student generalization, representation-level transfer that preserves structure beyond logits, and methods that remove dependence on the teacher's training data. However, KD is not a single monolithic recipe — optimization dynamics, teacher-student mismatch, and interactions with other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing or fairness constraints) materially affect outcomes. I argue that practitioners should treat KD as a collection of complementary approaches (logit regularization, feature mimicking, contrastive alignment, data- or generator-based sample synthesis, and adaptive teacher selection) and choose combinations appropriate to their constraints (data availability, privacy, compute, heterogeneity). This perspective explains why simpler or even teacher-free approaches can match standard KD in many settings, and why representation- and adaptation-oriented variants expand KD’s applicability to domain adaptation, federated and graph models.

papers_seen.author: Webb
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of practical techniques for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining predictive performance. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft output distributions, intermediate features, attention/relations) and how transfer is performed (offline teacher supervision, multi-teacher curricula, self-distillation, or data-free synthesis). Effective compression pipelines align distillation objectives with student capacity, leverage task- and data-aware strategies, and combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Key challenges include teacher–student mismatch, limited or no access to original training data, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behaviors, and robustness under domain shift; addressing these issues requires careful selection of distilled signals, adaptive teacher weighting, and data-generation or augmentation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transform large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, methods include soft-target (logit) distillation, feature and representation matching, layer-mapping strategies for large pretrained models, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and training-time variants such as online or co-distillation. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance while yielding substantial savings in memory, latency, and energy; however, outcomes depend on teacher–student compatibility, access to task data, which signals are transferred, and training protocol choices. Key open problems include robust cross-domain transfer, handling teacher errors and low-frequency phenomena, and reducing distillation cost when teachers are large or data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Guerrero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression: Powerful, Practical, but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully—selecting which teacher signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining KD with complementary compression primitives—KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks. However, KD is not a universal panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and careful handling of robustness, fairness, and optimization interactions. I argue that KD should serve as the default first-line method in compression toolkits, but practitioners must treat it as a design paradigm that is complemented by targeted validation and additional compression methods where needed.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques that transfer information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving predictive performance. KD methods differ in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational structure) and how training proceeds (offline teacher supervision, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, or data-free synthesis). Practical deployments combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and require attention to teacher–student alignment, data availability, and task-specific choices. Empirical evidence shows KD reliably yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks, but success depends on optimization dynamics, the choice of distilled signals, and constraints such as access to original training data or deployment hardware.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal information from teacher models. KD methods range from matching softened teacher logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure, and are commonly combined with complementary engineering strategies (architecture design, pretraining of compact models, quantization, and data augmentation). Empirical evidence shows distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision and language tasks while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability and augmentation, and the relative strength and role of the teacher; these choices shape practical tradeoffs in robustness, fairness, and cross-distribution generalization.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods that transfers knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models so deployments meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD encompasses soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate-representation and attention matching, relational or structural transfer, self- and multi-teacher schemes, and data-side interventions (including data-free and few-shot protocols). When combined with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and appropriate data and optimization practices, KD yields compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision and language tasks. Open problems include principled theory of when KD helps, reliably transferring robustness and fairness, handling distribution shift and rare or low-frequency phenomena in NLP, and automated student design under strict resource budgets.

papers_seen.author: Warren
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Position and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as the practical core of model compression for deep learning and NLP: a multifaceted toolkit that reliably reduces inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance when combined with careful design choices. KD succeeds because it can transfer soft predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and relational structure, and because it composes naturally with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and data strategies (augmentation, synthesis, and privacy-preserving proxies). However, KD is not a universal cure — its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, access to appropriate data (or viable data-free alternatives), and explicit handling of robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy constraints. Practitioners should therefore treat KD as a core, configurable element of compression pipelines and pair it with targeted engineering, diagnostics, and domain-aware choices to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels. Practitioners use a spectrum of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals) and training paradigms (offline, online, multi-teacher, and data‑free) together with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation) to meet latency, memory, privacy, and deployment constraints. Empirical work shows that thoughtfully designed distillation pipelines often preserve most teacher performance while substantially reducing compute, but success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability or synthesis strategies, alignment of internal representations, and optimization choices. Important open issues include reliable distillation without original data, preserving robustness and fairness under compression, and principled criteria for selecting distillation signals and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD encompasses logit-level soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational or ensemble signals, and many practical variants (online, self-distillation, data-free). When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student co-design, KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for classification, sequence tasks, retrieval, and generative systems. However, KD is not universally effective: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and distributional match, and the choice of distillation signals; open problems include reliable distillation without original data, preserving low-frequency or rare behaviors in NLP, and avoiding transfer of undesirable properties such as biases or fragility.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, distillation methods—ranging from matching teacher soft targets to aligning intermediate features or using data-free synthesis—enable substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical deployments combine distillation with architecture-aware choices (pruning, replacement, or search), multi-teacher or online schemes, and task-aware data strategies. Success depends on teacher quality, choice of transfer targets, data availability, and handling of mismatches; when carefully designed, distillation yields compact, robust models suitable for resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. KD operates through complementary mechanisms — soft-target regularization, internal representation transfer, and architecture- or data-aware adaptations — and integrates naturally with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design). When applied with attention to teacher quality, signal selection (logits vs features), and data constraints, distillation produces efficient models that are usable in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployments. However, KD has systematic limitations tied to teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, and potential transfer of undesirable behaviors, which motivate principled combinations of KD recipes and deployment-aware practices.

papers_seen.author: Medina
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, practical toolkit for compressing large neural networks into smaller, deployable models. Methods extend beyond simple soft-target (logit) matching to include alignment of intermediate representations, attention maps, relational structure, and architecture-aware adaptations. In practice KD is combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data‑free approaches), and training curricula (annealing, multi-teacher or online schedules). Empirical work across vision and language shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and design choices that affect robustness, fairness, and generalization under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Current Understandings of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used model compression paradigm in which a smaller student model is trained to capture the behavior of a larger teacher model. It has been applied across domains (vision, NLP, recommender systems, medical imaging) to reduce model size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Work in the field explores what is transferred (soft outputs, internal representations, feature relations), how to improve transfer (adversarial samples, contrastive objectives, structural transformations), and how to address practical constraints (absence of original data, domain shift, privacy, fairness and robustness). Empirical results show KD often yields substantial memory and runtime benefits with modest accuracy loss and can be combined with pruning, quantization and architecture search. Yet KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, imperfect teacher signals, and mismatches between teacher and student capacity can limit how closely a student matches a teacher; research continues into theoretical explanations and robust, data-efficient methods.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the central, practical toolkit for compressing large deep models into deployable students in both deep learning and NLP. KD provides flexible supervision (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, ensemble signals) and interoperates with complementary techniques (architecture search, pruning, quantization, data synthesis). When used systematically—selecting what to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity, leveraging data-aware or data-free strategies, and integrating KD into broader compression pipelines—KD enables strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployments. At the same time, careful attention to teacher quality, rare-token preservation, robustness, and domain shift is required to avoid predictable failure modes and to maximize real-world utility.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Perkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the past decade, a broad toolkit has emerged—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free or synthesized-data strategies, and task- or device-aware integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, handling limited or private data, and co-designing teacher and student architectures. While distillation routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks, remaining challenges include preserving rare or safety-critical behaviors, avoiding transfer of undesirable biases, ensuring robustness under distribution shift, and producing principled guidance for method selection and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and versatile approach for producing compact models by transferring richer supervision from large teacher models into smaller students. When implemented as a flexible design pattern—combining softened outputs, intermediate representation matching, attention or relational signals, and appropriate data strategies—KD frequently yields students that approach teacher performance while reducing inference cost. Its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, pre-training and data availability, and evaluation under realistic distributional and fairness constraints. I argue KD should be treated as a core component of compression pipelines but applied with explicit safeguards and complementary techniques to ensure robust, privacy-aware, and domain-appropriate deployment.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide effective ways to reduce the computational and memory costs of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Approaches span soft-target (logit) distillation, feature- and layer-level matching, data-augmentation and data-free techniques, and multi-teacher or teacher-optimization strategies. Recent work emphasizes task-aware alignment between teacher and student representations, augmentation schemes that improve teacher-student consistency, and training teachers that are explicitly optimized to help downstream students, enabling more reliable deployment in low-resource and privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Galvan
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Pragmatic Design Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable family of methods that enables deployment of high-performing but resource-hungry models by training compact students that retain much of teacher behavior. KD delivers major operational benefits — reduced inference latency, lower memory footprint, and greater deployability under compute, bandwidth, and privacy constraints — but it is not a one-size-fits-all cure. Real-world success requires treating KD as a design paradigm: choose what form of knowledge to transfer (soft targets, intermediate features, relations), co-design teacher and student capacities, address data limitations (via targeted augmentation or synthetic data), and explicitly manage robustness, fairness, and rare-token behaviors. When combined with complementary compression tools and careful evaluation, KD is the central practical strategy for producing efficient, reliable models for modern NLP and deep-learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels — output logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure — and are commonly combined with architecture-level compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and training strategies (online co-training, curriculum schedules, synthetic-data protocols). Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while improving latency and memory usage, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and appropriate choice of transfer signal. Ongoing challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, and operating in data-limited or privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Salinas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Patterns
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated approach for producing compact models by transferring richer supervision from larger teacher models to smaller students. KD encompasses multiple transfer signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational maps), supports various training regimes (offline teacher-to-student, online/co‑distillation, multi‑teacher ensembles), and composes with structural compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Its practical success depends on teacher quality and compatibility, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthetic-data strategies, and explicit evaluation for robustness and fairness. Treating KD as a design pipeline—selecting appropriate signals, aligning representations, adapting data strategies, and combining with complementary compression—yields students that meet real‑world deployment constraints while reducing common failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical toolkit for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, success hinges on what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, or relational signals), how teacher–student mismatches and data constraints are handled, and how distillation is combined with complementary strategies (pretraining, architecture choices, and data-centric methods). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can preserve most teacher performance under many conditions, but open problems remain in data-free and privacy-preserving settings, robust transfer under heterogeneity, and automated trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Strategy for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a unifying strategy that addresses model size, inference latency, domain shifts, multimodal transfer, privacy, and training efficiency. By transferring supervisory signals, intermediate representations, or relational structure from larger or more capable systems, KD enables compact student models to retain much of the performance of cumbersome teachers while meeting practical deployment constraints. When combined with task-aware architecture search, layer-mapping techniques, and online or domain-aware protocols, distillation offers a principled path to build small, fast, and adaptable models across diverse settings.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a family of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving task performance. KD methods range from transferring softened teacher outputs to matching intermediate representations or relational structure, and they are applied across modalities including language, vision, speech, and multimodal architectures. Practical deployments combine KD with architecture-aware transformations, low-precision numerics, data synthesis, and multi-stage training to address constraints such as limited data, heterogeneous devices, and privacy. While KD often yields strong empirical gains, success depends on choices about what to transfer, data availability and provenance, student architecture design, and optimization strategy; core open problems include handling teacher errors, preserving rare or fine-grained behavior, and reliably distilling across domain or architecture gaps.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, practical approach to compressing large deep models for deployment, but its success depends on careful choices about what is distilled, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data and deployment constraints are handled. KD is most effective when combined with architecture- and task-aware decisions and complementary compression techniques, and practitioners must evaluate distillation under realistic distributional, privacy, and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, high-capacity models to smaller, deployable models. Across computer vision, speech, recommendation, and natural language tasks, KD has been used to reduce inference cost while retaining most of the teacher model's performance. Research has advanced along several complementary axes: (1) methods that shape what is transferred (logits, hidden representations, attention or task-specific signals), (2) how the transfer is performed (layer-wise, multi-teacher, adversarial or student-aware training), (3) strategies to cope with limited or no access to original training data, and (4) techniques that preserve privacy and improve training efficiency. These lines of work show that careful alignment of objectives, attention to capacity gaps between teacher and student, and tailoring distillation to task and data regimes are critical for effective compression. Remaining challenges include robust cross-domain transfer, principled selection of what to distill for a target task, and maintaining robustness and fairness in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Bell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, System-Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable approach that should be treated as the first-line, system-level strategy for compressing large models into deployable students. When KD is applied as a design primitive — selecting which signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods and data strategies — it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across modalities. However, reliable deployment requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and robustness under distribution shift.
