papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. When combined with representation-level objectives, architecture-aware techniques, and deployment-aware protocols, KD preserves much of teacher performance while enabling real-world constraints such as latency, memory, and device heterogeneity to be met. Best practices include selecting appropriate distilled signals (beyond soft labels), pretraining or warming students, and aligning objectives with deployment constraints. Despite strong empirical success across modalities, open challenges remain in handling data heterogeneity, domain shift, privacy-sensitive settings, and the automated design of student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Lin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfers information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. KD encompasses soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention or relational alignment, multi-teacher and online strategies, and task- or data-aware adaptations. Practical compression typically combines KD with architecture-aware design, pretraining, data strategies (including data-free synthesis), and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, or layer skipping). Success depends on careful matching of distilled signals to the student architecture and deployment constraints; important open problems include handling teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift and heterogeneity, preserving rare or low-frequency information, and maintaining robustness and privacy in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, empirically effective strategy for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When treated as the first-line compression method and combined with complementary techniques (architecture design, pruning, quantization, data augmentation, or synthetic-data strategies), KD enables deployable students across modalities while also serving as a regularizer that can improve generalization. However, KD has well-documented failure modes — teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift, data-limited or privacy-constrained settings, and difficulties preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors — so practical deployment requires careful co-design of teacher signals, student capacity, and data protocols. The body of evidence supports KD as a central tool in compression pipelines but emphasizes hybrid workflows and targeted mitigations for its limits.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated framework that enables transferring predictive power from large, expensive models to smaller, deployable ones. KD supports diverse practical constraints — absent training data, limited downstream-task data, domain shifts, multi-task settings, and architectural mismatches — and couples naturally with automated model search and targeted feature imitation. By viewing KD as a family of techniques (logit transfer, feature mimicking, adversarial-sample guidance, synthetic-data distillation, and teacher-ensemble strategies) practitioners can compress models while retaining or even improving task-relevant inductive structure and generalization.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default Compression Strategy for Deep Learning and NLP: Rationale and Practical Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the default, first‑line strategy for compressing large neural models in deep learning and NLP because it provides flexible, task‑aware transfer channels that preserve predictive behavior while enabling complementary structural compression. KD excels when combined with architecture-aware design, representation-level alignment, and data strategies that address limited or private training data. A practical KD-first pipeline—selecting appropriate transfer signals, applying task-aware layer mappings, leveraging data-free or augmentation methods when needed, and composing KD with pruning/quantization—yields robust, high-compression students suitable for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Coleman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. KD methods range from matching softened output distributions to aligning intermediate features, attention patterns, and relational signals, and they are frequently combined with structural compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and recommendation tasks shows KD can produce compact models with strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, but its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, the choice of transferred signals, data availability (including data-free or few-shot scenarios), and careful optimization and evaluation. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a toolkit that must be tailored to task, data, and system constraints and augmented with diagnostics for robustness, fairness, and rare-token or out-of-distribution behavior.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A diverse set of KD mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature alignment, attention- and relation-based signals, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data synthesis—has been developed and combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many vision and language tasks, while remaining sensitive to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, domain shift, and robustness concerns. Practical pipelines therefore co-design student architectures, distillation targets, and data handling strategies to achieve the best trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Meza
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, system-level family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, compute, and privacy. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple softened-logit matching into many practical recipes — intermediate-feature and attention matching, relation-aware losses, multi-teacher schemes, online or co-distillation, and data-free or federated variants — and is most effective when combined with architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, compact pretraining) and task- or data-aware strategies. Empirical and analytic work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance and sometimes improve generalization, but outcomes depend critically on what knowledge is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and optimization dynamics; open challenges remain around robustness, rare-token and long-tail behavior, privacy, and principled student design.

papers_seen.author: French
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks KD has matured into a flexible toolkit—spanning softened-logit transfer, intermediate-representation and attention matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware or data-free variants—that, when combined with architecture-aware design and other compression primitives (pruning, quantization), enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while retaining much of a teacher's predictive power. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, availability and provenance of data, and evaluation of robustness, fairness, and distributional generalization. Ongoing challenges include reliable distillation under data scarcity or domain shift, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors in NLP, and avoiding transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: Practical, Theoretical, and Methodological Evidence for Efficient Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and mature approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from richer teacher models to compact students. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, vision, graph learning, and retrieval—KD enables substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while retaining most of the teacher's performance. Beyond pure compression, KD variants address practical deployment concerns: multi-teacher and confidence-aware schemes improve robustness to imperfect teachers; progressive and module-level replacement approaches enable deeper integrated compression; online/distillation-in-parallel techniques scale training and improve reproducibility; and targeted feature-distillation methods refine representational quality. Theory of wide networks provides guidance on when soft labels help and when mixing hard labels is beneficial. Together, empirical and theoretical work shows KD is a versatile, well-grounded toolbox for model compression and knowledge transfer in modern deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from teacher(s) to student(s). Advances span logit- and feature-based matching, multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, data-free and federated scenarios, and domain- or task-specific adaptations in NLP. Practical work shows KD can yield large reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance, but design choices (what to match, how to weight teachers, whether data are available, and deployment constraints) strongly affect outcomes. Remaining challenges include robustness to domain shift, privacy and communication constraints in distributed settings, and principled handling of teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Ashley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a pipeline—combining choice of distillation targets, student architecture design, pretraining, data strategies, and complementary compression steps—KD yields strong accuracy/efficiency trade-offs across vision and NLP. Yet KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and provenance of training data, and explicit design to preserve rare-token or domain-specific behavior. I argue KD should be the default first‑line method for model compression in deep learning and NLP while practitioners remain attentive to its failure modes and incorporate multi-teacher, domain‑aware, and data-aware remedies where appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Responsible Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile approach that compresses large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble consensus. KD enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance across modalities (NLP, speech, vision) and tasks. Its practical success depends on the choice of distilled signals, data strategies, and teacher-student design; when combined with augmentation, ensemble guidance, or privacy-aware mechanisms, KD supports real-world deployment while requiring safeguards against bias, privacy leakage, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical, Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic family of techniques for turning large, high‑performing models into smaller, deployable ones. When treated as a system‑level design choice rather than a single loss term, KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and inference cost while often preserving much of a teacher's predictive power. Realizing these benefits in practice requires choosing what knowledge to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacities, and combining KD with complementary practices such as compact pre‑training, data augmentation, or privacy‑aware data synthesis. KD is powerful but not universal: its effectiveness depends on data availability, teacher quality, and deployment constraints, so practitioners must evaluate and adapt distillation strategies to their task and context.

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing compact, efficient deep models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students. Across domains — vision, generation, control, and natural language tasks — KD enables large portions of teacher performance to be retained while enabling dramatic reductions in inference cost, memory footprint, and power consumption. When used thoughtfully (choice of distillation signal, teacher–student compatibility, and data strategy), KD integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and privacy- or data-constrained workflows to produce production-ready compact models. Equally important are mitigations for risks such as bias transfer, degraded robustness under domain shift, and failures when original training data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: The Strengths and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into deployable, efficient students across modalities. Empirical work shows KD can preserve task performance while drastically reducing size and compute, but its success depends on choices of what and how to transfer, availability and provenance of data, and training dynamics. Advances in feature-matching, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, data-free synthesis, and robustness-aware distillation expand KD's applicability but do not eliminate core challenges—optimization barriers, distribution heterogeneity, privacy constraints, and potential transfer of unwanted behaviors. A careful, task-aware combination of techniques is therefore required to realize reliable, compact models for production use.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are a widely adopted toolkit for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy of larger teachers. Research across vision and language characterizes KD as a family of methods—transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, relational structure, or training signals via specialized curricula or online exchanges—and shows that KD integrates naturally with pretraining, architecture design, and deployment-aware strategies. Practical success depends on matching the choice of knowledge (what to transfer), the teacher-student pairing (capacity and architecture), available data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and optimization curricula to the target task and constraints. While KD routinely yields substantial runtime and memory gains with modest accuracy loss, open challenges remain in handling domain shift, rare-token transfer in NLP, optimization mismatch, and large-scale or privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Methods and Challenges in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across vision, generative modeling, and NLP, researchers have developed logit- and feature-level distillation, task-specific adaptations, multi-teacher schemes, and teacher-optimization strategies to improve student accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. Work also focuses on constraints arising in distributed and privacy-preserving settings, on preserving rare or fine-grained information, and on adapting distillation to complex tasks such as detection, generation, and dense prediction. Practical systems combine architectural choices, training curricula, and distilled supervision to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, more efficient students to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD strategies vary in what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate representations, relations), how it is transferred (logit matching, feature-mimicking, projector layers, contrastive objectives, adversarial losses), and in deployment settings (data-available, data-free, federated or distributed, and online). Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, distilled students frequently recover much of teacher performance while enabling practical gains in speed and memory; however, method choice, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and distributional shifts materially affect outcomes, and open problems remain in preserving rare-token behavior, transferring robustness and fairness, and compressing across heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical, flexible route to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. KD spans multiple mechanisms — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation transfer, layer-wise or progressive replacement, privacy- and data-aware variants — and can be combined with structural compression such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is highly effective in many realistic settings but is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, what form of knowledge is transferred, data availability (including few-shot or privacy-constrained scenarios), and careful optimization and evaluation. Viewed as a central yet context-sensitive tool, KD should be a default component of compression pipelines, applied in concert with complementary methods and guarded by targeted diagnostics for robustness and rare-token or out-of-distribution behavior.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is the most practical, flexible, and widely applied approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and language tasks. KD brings together soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware strategies into a single, adaptable pipeline that can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet real-world deployment constraints. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, its reliability depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these concerns makes KD a central component of robust, system-level compression workflows rather than a one-shot recipe.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central family of techniques for compressing and accelerating deep models by transferring information from larger (teacher) models or training dynamics into smaller (student) models. Across domains and modalities—vision, graph data, speech, and natural language—KD variants address different constraints: limited data or privacy, distributed training, domain shift, and task-specific requirements (e.g., ranking, generation, or sequence modeling). Mechanistically, KD leverages richer supervisory signals than hard labels (soft targets, intermediate features, relational structure, or training trajectories) to regularize students and often yields students that approach teacher accuracy while improving latency and memory. Recent work has clarified connections between KD and other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing), introduced teacher-free and self-distillation approaches, explored the role of data augmentation and feature projectors, and adapted KD to federated, ensemble, and cross-task settings. Empirical results across tasks show KD can enable large compression/acceleration gains with modest performance loss and, in some settings, even improve generalization and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful, Central, but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their predictive power. KD methods span soft‑label/ logits transfer, intermediate‑feature and attention matching, adversarial and data‑free approaches, and teacher‑student co‑training or meta‑learned teachers. When thoughtfully designed — selecting appropriate distillation targets, aligning teacher and student capacities, and addressing data availability and robustness requirements — KD enables practical deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity constraints. However, KD is not universally successful: its effectiveness depends on architecture compatibility, quality and coverage of data (or of synthetic surrogates), and task‑specific choices, so practitioners must evaluate distillation under realistic conditions and adopt best practices tailored to their constraints.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple logits-matching into a broad toolkit that includes intermediate-representation and attention matching, ensemble and multi-teacher guidance, data- and teacher-free variants, and system-level integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely yields strong efficiency–performance trade-offs when teacher–student capacity, distillation targets, and data strategies are chosen thoughtfully, but its effectiveness is context-dependent: data availability, distributional shift, architecture compatibility, and task-specific behaviors can limit transfer and require tailored evaluation and mitigation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a family of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving task performance. KD methods range from transferring softened teacher outputs to matching intermediate representations or relational structure, and they are applied across modalities including language, vision, speech, and multimodal architectures. Practical deployments combine KD with architecture-aware transformations, low-precision numerics, data synthesis, and multi-stage training to address constraints such as limited data, heterogeneous devices, and privacy. While KD often yields strong empirical gains, success depends on choices about what to transfer, data availability and provenance, student architecture design, and optimization strategy; core open problems include handling teacher errors, preserving rare or fine-grained behavior, and reliably distilling across domain or architecture gaps.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. A broad family of methods—matching soft outputs (logits), imitating intermediate features and attention, ensembling or multi-teacher fusion, self-distillation, and data-free or few-shot synthesis—has been developed and routinely combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work across vision, language, and related domains shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while reducing memory, compute, and latency. However, practical success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and optimization dynamics; open problems include preserving rare-token behavior, robustness, privacy, and principled student design for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core technique for making large neural models deployable: by transferring richer supervision from high-capacity teacher models to compact students, KD enables substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while often preserving or even improving generalization. Best results arise when distillation strategies are matched to deployment constraints and student capacity—combining logits and representational objectives, co-designing teacher and student, using appropriate data-augmentation or synthetic-data strategies, and integrating structural compression like pruning or module replacement. Although challenges remain (teacher imperfections, low-frequency token fidelity, data-free settings, and distribution shift), a set of practical, complementary methods yields robust pathways to efficient models across NLP and other domains.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Multi-purpose Strategy for Model Compression and Robust Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD supports domain adaptation, latency-aware architecture transformations, robustness transfer, and interpretable model surrogates. When combined with careful training protocols (e.g., multi-teacher schemes, domain adaptation, or targeted regularization), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models in resource- and latency-constrained or safety-critical settings across vision, speech, 3D perception, and natural language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Favoring Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical, versatile pathway to produce compact models that preserve much of the performance of larger teachers while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When treated as a design paradigm—choosing what form of knowledge to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression primitives—KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade‑offs across modalities. KD should be adopted as the default first‑line compression method in deep learning and NLP while being applied with careful safeguards for data, robustness, and task alignment.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile technique for shrinking large neural models while preserving much of their predictive power. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and easier deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings. When combined with teacher ensembles, online or self-distillation, task-adaptive search, and careful handling of soft labels and data augmentation, distillation can deliver near-teacher accuracy while addressing scalability, robustness, and domain transfer concerns. I argue that knowledge distillation should be a first-line approach for model compression in modern NLP pipelines, supplemented by principled choices about teachers, data, and optimization to realize its full benefits.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A broad family of KD techniques—logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, multi-teacher and self-distillation schedules, and data-aware or data-free synthesis—has been developed and frequently combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Empirical results across vision and NLP show that carefully designed distillation pipelines recover much of the teacher’s performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but persistent challenges remain in handling data scarcity or privacy constraints, aligning heterogeneous teacher–student capacities, and preserving robustness, fairness, and long-tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Benson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a reliable and versatile technique for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when combined with architecture-aware design, layer- and representation-level alignment, and appropriate data strategies. However, its success depends on careful choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle distributional or data-availability gaps; KD therefore belongs at the center of compression pipelines rather than as a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features/attention, relational or structural signals) and can be applied in offline, online, ensemble, or data-constrained settings. Empirical results across vision, speech, and language show that appropriately designed distillation pipelines can deliver large efficiency gains with modest loss (and sometimes gains) in accuracy, but success depends on choices about what is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical deployments typically combine KD with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and require design attention to robustness, domain shift, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression — Powerful but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the central, first‑line strategy for compressing large deep models for deployment in deep learning and NLP. KD provides flexible transfer channels (soft targets, intermediate features, attention and relational signals) that, when combined with architecture-aware choices, data strategies, and complementary structural compression (pruning, quantization, search), yield compact students that retain much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, teacher–student capacity and alignment, availability or synthesis of suitable data, and careful optimization and evaluation under distribution shift, fairness, and privacy constraints. Practitioners should adopt KD as a toolbox—selecting signals and curricula, aligning representations, and composing KD with other compression methods—while tracking open problems in theoretical guarantees, data-free and private distillation, and robust transfer of rare or domain‑specific behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become the primary, practical method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD unifies multiple training strategies—soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, multi-teacher schedules, and data-free synthesis—enabling substantial reductions in inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search) and when its objectives and data regimes are chosen to match student capacity and deployment constraints. Despite its strengths, KD has known weaknesses, including sensitivity to teacher–student mismatch, degradation under data heterogeneity, and risks of transferring undesirable behaviors; addressing these requires careful protocol design, selective transfer of teacher signals, and hybrid pipelines that integrate KD with data-centric and architecture-centric interventions.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques provide practical pathways to convert large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. Empirically, KD can transfer predictive behavior and internal representations to students that retain much of the teacher’s effectiveness, especially when combined with complementary strategies such as pre-training of compact architectures, careful layer or module mapping, and data-management methods. Successful pipelines trade off accuracy, latency, and model size while navigating constraints such as limited or private data and domain shift. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness (including rare-token behavior), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and developing principled data-free or privacy-preserving distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other forms of teacher knowledge. Across vision and language tasks KD has enabled practical reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on what form of knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student representations are aligned, the availability and selection of data for distillation, and complementary compression techniques such as low-precision numerics, pruning, or architecture adaptation. Remaining challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, reliable distillation without original data, robustness and fairness under compression, and principled methods for matching heterogeneous teacher–student pairs.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD encompasses soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, relational or contrastive objectives, self- and multi-teacher schemes, and data-aware variants (including data-free and federated protocols). Empirical evidence shows KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across vision, NLP, speech, graph, and multi-task settings, but success depends on student capacity, teacher–student alignment, available data (or generators), and attention to robustness, privacy, and long-tail phenomena. Practical pipelines treat KD as one component of compression that should be combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, and careful training curricula.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teacher's performance. When combined with complementary strategies — such as careful layer mapping, pre-training of compact models, multi-teacher schedules, privacy-aware mechanisms, and synthetic-data techniques — distillation addresses the principal deployment barriers of modern deep networks: inference cost, data access constraints, and heterogeneous compute environments. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be treated not as a single recipe but as a flexible toolkit that can be adapted to the needs of NLP and general deep learning applications to produce compact, robust, and privacy-conscious models.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Dalton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied deliberately — choosing what to transfer (logits, features, attention), aligning teacher and student capacity, and combining KD with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search — KD yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across vision and language tasks. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher quality, data availability (including data‑free or privacy‑constrained scenarios), and careful design around teacher–student mismatch and task-specific objectives. Responsible, task-aware application of KD, integrated into system-level compression pipelines, produces the most reliable operational outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Path to Compact, High-Quality Models in NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models for deployment. Across NLP and other modalities, distillation enables lightweight architectures to retain much of a teacher's performance while supporting additional compression techniques (pruning, quantization) and privacy-respecting or data-free workflows. However, distillation outcomes depend strongly on teacher–student compatibility, the form of distilled knowledge (logits, features, attention), access to data, and optimization choices. Best results arise when distillation is integrated with appropriate pre-training, architectural adapters (projectors or attention alignment), and, when necessary, data synthesis or domain adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Haynes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, general-purpose approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. When applied with attention to what knowledge is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), to teacher–student capacity alignment, and to data constraints, KD routinely yields substantial improvements in inference latency and memory while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: it carries risks (transfer of bias, privacy leakage, reduced robustness on distribution shift and rare tokens) and requires complementary techniques (task-aware objectives, architecture design, dataset strategies, and robustness/privacy safeguards) to be reliable in production. I argue KD should be treated as the first‑line, default strategy for model compression in deep learning and NLP, used proactively alongside targeted mitigations for its limits and with careful empirical validation.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Failure Modes, and Practical Recipes
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, recommendation, and NLP. KD techniques range from simple logits matching to representation-level transfer, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial sample synthesis, and progressive module replacement. While many distillation recipes recover most of a teacher’s accuracy and enable large efficiency gains, the success of KD depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or absent training data. Careful design—matching distillation targets to student capacity, mitigating transferred errors, and combining distillation with complementary compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search)—yields robust, efficient models for practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has branched from simple soft-target matching into a family of methods including logits and feature matching, layer-wise and task-aware distillation, self- and online-distillation, data-free or adversarial sample synthesis, and strategies for low-precision or few-shot deployment. Practical success depends on matching the distilled signal to student capacity, handling limited or private data, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning and quantization). Open challenges remain around robust data-free distillation, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, preventing harmful bias transfer, and building stronger theoretical predictions of when and how distillation succeeds.

papers_seen.author: Castaneda
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Patterns, and Practical Caveats
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile toolkit that transfers richer supervision from larger or heterogeneous teacher models into smaller students to reduce inference cost while retaining task performance. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals), composes with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design), and can be adapted to domain-specific settings (generative models, recommenders, distributed training). Its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data alignment, choice of signals to transfer, and mitigation strategies for robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy. When applied with principled design—matching distilled signals to student capacity, using teacher-aware curricula, and combining with other compression tools—KD frequently yields production-ready efficiency gains, but it is not a universal remedy and requires careful engineering to avoid failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Andrews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals—and are often combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design). Across vision and language tasks, distillation commonly yields large efficiency gains with modest performance loss when teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and evaluation under realistic deployment constraints are addressed. Important ongoing challenges include data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, robustness and fairness under compression, preserving rare-token behaviors in NLP, and principled choices about which signals to transfer.
