papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Practical Extensions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring teacher knowledge during training. Beyond the original soft-target paradigm, a rich family of methods has emerged: feature- and attention-based matching, many-to-many layer alignment, self-distillation, and data- or representation-based distillation tailored to tasks such as object detection, translation, and pre-trained language model compression. KD also acts as a regularizer related to label smoothing and can be adapted to provide differential privacy, federated model aggregation, and improved adversarial robustness. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the power of KD to improve student generalization and important limitations—optimization difficulties, mismatches in internal representations, and distributional effects on rare tokens or classes—that guide current research directions.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Practices and Open Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques reduce model size and inference cost by transferring information from a high-capacity source (teacher) to a smaller target (student). Across vision, speech, and NLP, practitioners combine logit-based supervision, feature imitation, data augmentation, and architectural or precision changes to preserve performance while shrinking computation. Recent work emphasizes (1) the role of pre-training for compact models, (2) task- and modality-specific distillation recipes, (3) data-availability and privacy constraints that motivate data-free or augmentation-based approaches, and (4) designing teachers or training procedures that improve transfer. These trends point toward hybrid pipelines that integrate pre-training, augmentation, and teacher-student co-design to get robust, efficient models for real-world deployments.

papers_seen.author: Dodson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of distillation objectives—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention- and channel-guided losses, relational/contrastive signals, and self- or multi-teacher regimes—can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to trade accuracy for latency, memory, and power. Practical success depends on aligning teacher signals to student capacity, access to (or synthesis of) suitable training data, and mitigation of optimization, fairness, and robustness risks. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, representative methods, practical recommendations, and open challenges for applying distillation in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Suarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, widely applicable tool for shrinking large deep models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. When combined with complementary practices — careful teacher selection or adaptation, pre-training of compact architectures, feature-level matching, and privacy- or data-aware workflows — KD yields most of the practical benefits of compression while exposing clear trade-offs and failure modes. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the backbone of model compression pipelines, but that realizing reliable production gains requires principled choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Flores
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones. KD offers multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals) and can be combined with complementary compression methods and data strategies to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful design choices; KD should therefore be treated as a core element of a compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all solution.

papers_seen.author: Branch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of methods for transferring information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD encompasses a range of transferred signals (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention/relational patterns, and ensemble outputs), operates under multiple training regimes (offline, online, multi‑teacher, and data‑free), and composes naturally with structural compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Empirical evidence across vision, speech, and language shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and provenance, and attention to robustness, rare-token preservation, and fairness. Open challenges include reliable data‑free distillation, principled signal selection for heterogeneous architectures, and preserving safety‑critical behaviours under compression.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is the most practical, flexible, and widely applied approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and language tasks. KD brings together soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware strategies into a single, adaptable pipeline that can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet real-world deployment constraints. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, its reliability depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these concerns makes KD a central component of robust, system-level compression workflows rather than a one-shot recipe.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression: Capabilities, Limits, and Prescriptions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical evidence across vision and NLP shows KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs, but reliable deployment requires treating distillation as a core element within a broader compression pipeline rather than as a single recipe. Success depends on choosing what to transfer (logits, features, attentions, relational signals), aligning teacher and student architectures and capacities, handling data constraints or privacy requirements, and combining distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design). I argue KD should be regarded as the central practical strategy for model compression, guided by principled selection of distillation targets and integration with deployment-aware methods to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a multifaceted approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with attention to which signals are transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention), the teacher–student relationship, data availability, and deployment constraints, KD yields substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher behavior. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on capacity alignment, data and distributional match, and careful objective design. Practical adoption therefore requires selecting KD variants that fit task and system constraints and combining KD with complementary techniques (pretraining, data augmentation, multi-teacher signals, or architecture co-design) to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Atkinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably yields compact models that retain much of a larger teacher’s performance when applied with attention to what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, and data availability. KD works through multiple mechanisms—soft-target regularization, representation transfer, and ensemble-derived ‘‘dark knowledge’’—and its strengths are maximized when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and task-aware training curricula. However, KD is not a universal solution: practical deployments must address limits including distribution shift, rare-token behavior, privacy-sensitive or data-free scenarios, and potential transfer of undesirable teacher behavior. I therefore argue that KD should be treated as the practical core of hybrid compression pipelines, selected and tuned according to deployment constraints and supplemented with methods that mitigate its known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation trains smaller student models to capture the behavior of larger teacher models, enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, and privacy while often preserving much of teacher performance. Its practical effectiveness arises from multiple complementary mechanisms (soft targets, intermediate representation transfer, and data or architecture adaptations) and from combining distillation with structural compression techniques. However, distillation’s success is contingent on choices about teacher–student pairing, the provenance and availability of data, the distilled signals and training schedules, and deployment constraints such as federated or privacy-sensitive settings. A principled, task-aware approach that blends appropriate distillation objectives, data strategies (including data-free methods when necessary), and complementary compression methods yields the best tradeoffs between compactness and retained performance.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants transfer information via softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals, and adversarially or synthetically generated inputs. When combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, or data strategies, KD supports deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, success depends on careful matching of what is transferred to student capacity, handling data scarcity or distribution shift, and mitigating propagation of teacher errors. This synthesis summarizes common mechanisms, representative algorithmic families, empirical patterns, and actionable recommendations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Responsible Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring useful predictive and representational knowledge from teacher models to students. When combined with complementary techniques (e.g., layer mapping, multi-teacher weighting, data-free synthesis, pruning, and quantization) and guided by student-aware design and fairness/robustness constraints, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of a teacher's accuracy. Practical deployment of KD requires attention to data availability, teacher quality, and domain-specific constraints to avoid propagating undesirable behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Focused Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for producing compact models by transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students. Methods extend beyond matching softened output distributions to include intermediate-feature imitation, attention or relational alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher ensembles, and data-free or synthetic-data procedures. Best practices combine representation-aware objectives, student-aware architecture choices, and data strategies (pretraining, augmentation, or synthetic data) and often pair KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work across vision, speech, and NLP demonstrates KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but known limitations remain around domain shift, rare-token behavior, robustness, and privacy-sensitive or data-limited settings.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, broadly applicable family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their predictive power. KD enables large gains in inference speed, reduced memory footprint, and practical deployment under latency, compute, and privacy constraints. However, straightforward distillation can transfer undesirable properties and can underperform when data is limited or teacher–student mismatches are large. To realize KD's full potential practitioners should combine soft-target transfer with representation matching, targeted data augmentation or data-free synthesis, careful teacher design (including ensembles or student-aware teachers), and explicit robustness or privacy-aware objectives. These combined practices produce compact models that are accurate, efficient, and more robust for real-world NLP and deep-learning deployments.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expressive models to smaller, efficient models to enable practical deployment without excessive loss in performance. These methods include matching teacher soft outputs, feature-level alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and architecture-aware strategies for heterogeneous settings. Across domains—vision, speech, NLP, and recommender systems—distillation is used both to compress models for latency and memory constraints and to inject complementary knowledge (e.g., cross-task or cross-modal signals). Empirical work shows that careful design choices (e.g., mixing hard/soft targets, projector modules, or student-aware teacher training) and task-specific adaptations address common pitfalls such as information loss on rare tokens or domain shifts. Open directions include stronger theoretical understanding, robustness under imperfect teachers, and principled integration with quantization, federated settings, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Dependent Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a central, practical tool for compressing large models into efficient students while acknowledging that its effectiveness depends critically on task, data, teacher–student alignment, and deployment constraints. When combined with complementary techniques (architecture design, pruning, quantization, pretraining, and data strategies), KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs, but reliable production use requires deliberate signal selection, capacity-aware alignment, and privacy- or data-sensitive adaptations.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and natural language processing. A range of techniques—transferring soft logits, mimicking internal features or attention maps, layer-wise alignment, multi-teacher ensembles, and data-free or zero-shot approaches—enable tradeoffs between model size, latency, and retained performance. Distillation is applied not only for inference efficiency but also for domain adaptation, privacy-preserving federated training, and task-specific transfer. Practical success depends on careful teacher–student design, data considerations, and optimization strategies; ongoing challenges include robustness under domain shift, imperfect teachers, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Freeman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal signals so students meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. The field has evolved from soft-label matching to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-representation and attention alignment, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and data-free or adversarial sample synthesis; KD is frequently combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and domain-aware pretraining. Empirical and emerging theoretical work highlight both KD’s practical utility and its limits — success depends on teacher–student compatibility, availability and provenance of data, choice of transferred signals, and optimization curricula — motivating integrated pipelines and ongoing research on robustness, rare-token fidelity in sequence tasks, and privacy-preserving distillation.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller ones to reduce inference cost, improve deployability, or impart desirable properties (robustness, fairness, interpretability). Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, ensemble consensus, attention maps) and in what data is available (original training data, synthetic data, or no data). Practical systems combine KD with architecture-level compression (pruning, structured sparsity) and with training-time strategies (online or continual distillation, curriculum schedules) to trade off efficiency and accuracy. While KD yields strong empirical results across NLP, speech, vision, and generative models, open challenges remain in data-free settings, cross-domain generalization, preserving fairness and interpretability, and designing distillation objectives that best capture the teacher’s knowledge for a given task.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Kerr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Capabilities, Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically supported technique for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD methods range from matching softened logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational signals, and they can be combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization), architecture design, and data strategies (augmentation, synthesis, or data-free approaches). While KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, its success is context-dependent: it depends on teacher quality, teacher–student capacity alignment, and data provenance. Therefore KD should be treated as the central element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all remedy.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller students that are deployable under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, relational signals), aligning teacher and student architectures and tokenization, and combining KD with complementary techniques such as architecture search or targeted pruning—distillation routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance and sometimes even improve generalization. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on data availability, teacher quality and friendliness, domain shifts, and the specific form of knowledge chosen for transfer. Effective deployment therefore requires principled design of the distillation objective, curricula or annealing schedules, and safeguards for robustness and rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a heuristic into a central, practical toolkit for compressing large models and transferring behavior from high-capacity teachers into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative modeling, practitioners combine soft-label supervision, intermediate-representation matching, data- and privacy-aware strategies, and architecture-aware choices to trade accuracy for latency, memory, and power. KD is effective when paired with complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, synthetic-data generation, curriculum schedules), but its success depends critically on what form of knowledge is distilled, how data or augmentations are used, and how teacher–student capacity and domain mismatches are managed. Remaining challenges include robust data-free distillation, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, mitigating bias transfer, and firm theoretical characterizations that predict when and how distillation will work in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compress large models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. KD techniques that move beyond naive logit matching — for example by mimicking intermediate features, adapting teacher-student interactions to the task, or training teachers that are optimized for transfer — yield larger gains in both vision and language settings. KD also enables new training regimes (online and distributed) and can be combined with architecture search to produce task-aware compressed models. At the same time, interactions between KD and other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing) and the choice of what and how to transfer require careful design. Overall, KD is a mature and expanding toolkit that, when applied with methodical choices about knowledge type, teacher strategy, and training setup, provides an effective path to deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured into a core tool for shrinking large neural models into compact, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across domains — from language understanding and ranking to multimodal models and edge deployment — distillation enables trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and privacy that are otherwise difficult to achieve. However, consistent success requires more than naively matching teacher outputs: careful attention to student pre-training, layer alignment, task-aware selection of transferred signals, data augmentation, and deployment constraints (e.g., low-precision or federated scenarios) determines whether distillation yields practical gains. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be treated as a system-level design primitive rather than a single loss term, and it outlines methodological priorities to make distillation effective for NLP and deep learning practitioners.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Context‑Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical route to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD is both a compression mechanism and a training-time regularizer: when carefully designed it preserves much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and inference cost. However, KD’s success depends on choices about what to transfer (outputs, intermediate features, or both), how to align teacher and student architectures, what data are used (real, augmented, or synthetic), and whether deployment constraints (privacy, heterogeneity, federated settings) limit access to teacher data or models. A principled KD practice adapts targets, aligns representations where useful, addresses teacher–student mismatches, and recognizes scenarios where KD alone is insufficient.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary Compression Strategy for Practical Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the first-line strategy for compressing large deep models into deployable students: it reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal representations, is broadly applicable across modalities, and composes naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is not a silver bullet — its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, and how knowledge is represented and aligned — so production pipelines should combine KD with representation-aware objectives, student pretraining, and targeted data strategies to mitigate distributional and optimization pitfalls. When applied with these caveats, KD delivers strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs that make large pretrained models practical for constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. When treated as a system-level toolkit rather than a single loss term, KD reliably improves efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across modalities and tasks. Its success depends on deliberate choices about what is transferred (logits, features, attention, relations), how teacher and student are aligned, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression primitives and data strategies. Important open problems remain around distribution shift, low-frequency behaviors, privacy- and data-constrained settings, and principled data-free methods.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Effective Practices for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques reliably reduce large pretrained models to compact, efficient students suitable for deployment while preserving most of the teacher performance. Across NLP and multimodal tasks, practical compression requires strategies that (1) align representations at multiple levels, (2) focus on task-relevant information, and (3) handle limited or no access to original training data. Combining architecture-aware search, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, and improved input-side strategies (including data augmentation or data-free sample generation) yields compact models with strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs suitable for real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hunter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints. Across vision and language tasks KD methods—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature and relational alignment—consistently enable substantial reductions in compute and memory while recovering much of teacher accuracy when applied with attention to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization dynamics. Practical KD pipelines typically combine distilled signals with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adopt data-aware strategies (augmentation, synthetic-data generation, or data-free protocols) to address real-world deployment challenges. Key open problems include robustly preserving long-tail or rare behaviors, handling distribution shift and privacy constraints, and automating student design for strict resource budgets.

papers_seen.author: Salas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger, higher-capacity teacher models into compact student models. KD methods span output-level soft-target matching, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, multi-teacher or ensemble guidance, and data-aware or data-free training regimes. In practice KD is most effective when combined with complementary structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when the distillation strategy is matched to student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints. While distilled students frequently recover most of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, core challenges remain around distilling across heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors, ensuring robustness and fairness, and operating when original training data are private or unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, insights, and practical trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in latency-, memory-, and compute-constrained settings. Work across speech, NLP, vision, and graph domains demonstrates a spectrum of approaches: matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate features, progressively replacing modules, augmenting or synthesizing training data for better student generalization, and compressing ensembles into single models. Empirical results show substantial speed and size gains with modest accuracy loss when methods are carefully matched to task and architecture. Important themes include (1) the role of dark/soft labels vs. intermediate feature signals, (2) architectural or task-aware compression (including search), (3) techniques that increase the student’s exposure to informative training points (e.g., mixup or adversarial examples), and (4) distillation strategies tailored for ensembles or heterogeneous teacher–student pairs. Open challenges remain in principled sample selection, robust transfer of inductive biases, and automated trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Strategies, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central, pragmatic technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. When applied deliberately — choosing what form of knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle data and deployment constraints — KD routinely yields favorable tradeoffs between model compactness and retained performance. However, distillation is not automatic: data availability, teacher–student mismatches, and application-specific constraints (latency, privacy, heterogeneity) shape both achievable gains and failure modes. Best practice therefore combines representation-aware objectives, curriculum or annealing schedules, multi-teacher or ensemble guidance where helpful, and deployment-aware mechanisms such as data-free generation or privacy-preserving aggregation to realize robust, efficient students.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Effective Knowledge Distillation for Deployable Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool to compress large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, KD has enabled domain adaptation, model-size reduction, cross-lingual transfer, and deployment under resource constraints. Success depends on (1) aligning teacher and student inputs and intermediate representations, (2) choosing appropriate supervision signals (soft labels, intermediate-feature losses, attention-based guidance), (3) handling the absence of original training data when necessary, and (4) adapting compression to task and domain requirements. This review synthesizes empirical and methodological findings from recent studies to recommend principled KD choices for practitioners aiming to deploy compact, robust models in real-world NLP and related tasks.

papers_seen.author: Mccann
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller student models so students can meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, energy, privacy) while retaining much of teacher performance. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label (logit) matching to a toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive signals, multi-teacher and progressive schedules, and data-aware or data-free variants. KD is most effective when chosen signals, student architecture, and data strategies are matched to the task and deployment context and when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Important open problems remain around theory, robustness under distribution shift, preserving fine-grained or rare behaviors in language tasks, data-scarce or privacy-sensitive scenarios, and automated student design. This paper synthesizes empirical practices, mechanisms, theoretical insights, and practical guidance from recent studies to orient research and engineering choices for KD-based compression.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Flexible Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. When treated as a flexible toolkit rather than a single recipe, distillation enables compact models that preserve much of teacher performance across vision and language tasks. Combining KD with representation-aware objectives, teacher–student design, and deployment-aware techniques (pretraining, pruning, quantization, or federated protocols) addresses many real-world constraints while leaving open research questions about data-free distillation, cross-architecture representation transfer, and domain-generalization under aggressive compression.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Responsible Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring useful predictive and representational knowledge from teacher models to students. When combined with complementary techniques (e.g., layer mapping, multi-teacher weighting, data-free synthesis, pruning, and quantization) and guided by student-aware design and fairness/robustness constraints, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of a teacher's accuracy. Practical deployment of KD requires attention to data availability, teacher quality, and domain-specific constraints to avoid propagating undesirable behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary tools to shrink large deep models for deployment while retaining much of their predictive power. Across vision, speech and natural language processing, researchers have developed a range of approaches that operate at the level of logits (soft labels), intermediate representations, modules/layers, or training curricula, and have combined KD with complementary strategies such as architecture search, quantization, and generative replay. Empirical work shows that distilled students can often approach teacher performance while achieving large reductions in size and latency, but the effectiveness of different KD strategies depends strongly on task, data distribution, teacher strength, and practical constraints such as availability of original training data. Important challenges remain in transferring robustness, handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving rare-token behavior, and balancing bias–variance tradeoffs introduced by soft supervision.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.
