papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated pathway to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. KD encompasses multiple forms of transferred knowledge (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and operates across modes (offline, online, ensemble, data-free). When co‑designed with student architectures and combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs for vision and language models. However, practical success requires attention to teacher–student compatibility, data availability and provenance, and robustness to domain shift and rare behaviors. The method is best treated as a default, context‑aware tool that should be adapted—rather than assumed universal—for each deployment setting.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Understanding and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. It encompasses soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and training-time adaptations that account for student capacity and deployment constraints. In practice KD is combined with complementary methods (architecture search, pruning, quantization, data augmentation, and data-free synthesis) to meet latency, memory, or privacy requirements. KD is effective across vision, language, generative models, and view- or modality-specific tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student compatibility, available data, and careful choice of distillation objectives and schedules; open challenges remain in robustness, rare-token behavior, fairness, and theoretical guarantees.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teacher's performance. When combined with complementary strategies — such as careful layer mapping, pre-training of compact models, multi-teacher schedules, privacy-aware mechanisms, and synthetic-data techniques — distillation addresses the principal deployment barriers of modern deep networks: inference cost, data access constraints, and heterogeneous compute environments. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be treated not as a single recipe but as a flexible toolkit that can be adapted to the needs of NLP and general deep learning applications to produce compact, robust, and privacy-conscious models.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a predominant strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels. Across vision, language, speech, and other modalities, KD encompasses soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, relational and training-dynamics transfer, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. When integrated with architecture-level compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student co-design, KD enables substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss and can sometimes improve robustness or generalization. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align layers and representations, data availability, and safeguards for fairness and privacy; these constitute active areas of empirical and methodological work.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques provide a set of complementary strategies to transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller student models. Methods span matching output distributions (soft targets), imitating intermediate representations and attention, aligning layers, using multiple teachers or self-teaching schedules, and applying task- or data-aware procedures including data-free generation and low-precision adaptation. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance while gaining speed and memory efficiency, but outcomes depend on which knowledge is transferred, student capacity, data availability, and task specificity. Practical deployments combine distillation with architecture search, quantization, and curriculum or augmentation strategies to balance fidelity, robustness, and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students for deployment in deep learning and NLP. A broad family of KD techniques—ranging from softened-logit supervision to intermediate representation matching, attention- and feature-level imitation, many-to-many layer alignment, adversarial and data-free variants, and task- or device-aware architecture search—enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while often retaining most of the teacher's performance. Effective application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, whether and how to use original data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. Important open problems remain regarding theoretical understanding, robustness under distribution shift or imperfect teachers, and scalable private or data-free distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under memory, latency, or privacy constraints. The literature has converged on a set of recurring methods (soft-target/logit supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, multi-teacher schedules, data-free and privacy-aware protocols) and deployment practices (combining KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search). Empirical evidence demonstrates that appropriately designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional alignment. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors (especially in NLP), and principled teacher–student co-design and curricula for difficult tasks.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed as part of a broader compression pipeline that includes architecture-aware choices, data strategies, and complementary techniques such as pruning and quantization, KD reliably improves accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. Success requires attention to teacher–student capacity alignment, the nature and provenance of distillation data, and evaluation for robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy. KD is therefore best treated as a first-line, system-level primitive for compression rather than a universal cure: with careful design it yields high-impact, deployable compact models, but its limits must be managed through targeted engineering and auditing.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, System-Level Strategy for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD should be treated as the backbone of compression pipelines: when co-designed with student architectures, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques, it delivers most of the real-world gains in latency, memory, and deployability while exposing clear trade-offs and failure modes that must be managed.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from pre-trained teachers. The approach spans soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware or data-free workflows. Empirical results show KD often recovers much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and optimization protocols. Ongoing challenges include aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors, maintaining robustness and fairness under distribution shift, and operating when original training data is limited or unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential and Practical, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing parameter count and inference cost, but its reliability depends on choices about what to distill, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited, heterogeneous, or private data. Realistic deployment requires combining KD with complementary compression techniques, adapting the distillation signal to the task and student capacity, and evaluating robustness and privacy implications.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context-Dependent Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. It delivers meaningful trade-offs between model size, latency, and retained performance when paired with appropriate distillation targets, student-aware design, and complementary compression techniques. However, KD’s success is conditional: it depends on teacher-student capacity alignment, data availability (including privacy constraints), the choice of distilled signals (soft targets versus intermediate features), and optimization practices. Best outcomes arise from task-aware distillation pipelines that combine soft-target transfer, representation-level supervision, and pragmatic strategies such as data synthesis, augmentation, or architecture-aware adjustments.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Mcmillan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable but Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the original performance. KD has proven effective across modalities and tasks, and modern practice extends beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-representation alignment, multi-teacher fusion, data-free approaches, and training-time strategies that make teachers more amenable to transfer. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: distribution shifts, limited or absent training data, teacher–student mismatch, and adversarial concerns require complementary techniques and careful design. When combined with task-aware selection of distilled signals, student-friendly teacher training, and data- or representation-aware remedies, KD becomes a practical backbone for deployment under latency, compute, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression strategies have become central tools for shrinking large pretrained models into efficient deployable networks while preserving much of their performance. Methods range from transferring final-logit 'dark knowledge' to matching intermediate representations, attention maps, or feature distributions; from engineering compact student architectures to progressively replacing modules inside a single model. Applications span vision, speech, generative models, and NLP (including BERT compression and non-autoregressive translation), and extensions address scenarios with no access to original training data or heterogeneous, federated settings. Key trade-offs involve accuracy vs. size/latency, robustness and fairness, and the distributional assumptions needed for effective transfer. Important open problems include principled understanding of when and why distillation helps, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and reliably transferring robustness and inductive biases to small models.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become practical tools to reduce model size and computation while retaining much of the performance of large teachers. Across vision, speech, and natural language tasks, approaches include transferring soft logits, mimicking internal features or attention maps, layering/structural adaptations, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-preserving methods. Empirical results demonstrate that careful distillation can yield compact students that approach teacher accuracy and enable deployment in resource-constrained settings, but open challenges remain in robustness, task-specific distillation design, and distributed training dynamics.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving predictive performance. KD methods differ in what is transferred (softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals) and in training protocols (offline teacher supervision, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants). In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and when practitioner choices account for teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and target-task constraints. While KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across vision and language tasks, its limitations include sensitivity to optimization dynamics, degradation on rare or safety-critical behaviors, and challenges in data-free or privacy-constrained settings. The field offers pragmatic recipes—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning representations, and using data or synthetic surrogates—that produce deployable compact models, but outstanding research questions remain about principled teacher design, robustness under distribution shift, and data-free distillation quality.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central family of techniques for compressing and accelerating deep models by transferring information from larger (teacher) models or training dynamics into smaller (student) models. Across domains and modalities—vision, graph data, speech, and natural language—KD variants address different constraints: limited data or privacy, distributed training, domain shift, and task-specific requirements (e.g., ranking, generation, or sequence modeling). Mechanistically, KD leverages richer supervisory signals than hard labels (soft targets, intermediate features, relational structure, or training trajectories) to regularize students and often yields students that approach teacher accuracy while improving latency and memory. Recent work has clarified connections between KD and other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing), introduced teacher-free and self-distillation approaches, explored the role of data augmentation and feature projectors, and adapted KD to federated, ensemble, and cross-task settings. Empirical results across tasks show KD can enable large compression/acceleration gains with modest performance loss and, in some settings, even improve generalization and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Mccann
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller student models so students can meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, energy, privacy) while retaining much of teacher performance. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label (logit) matching to a toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive signals, multi-teacher and progressive schedules, and data-aware or data-free variants. KD is most effective when chosen signals, student architecture, and data strategies are matched to the task and deployment context and when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Important open problems remain around theory, robustness under distribution shift, preserving fine-grained or rare behaviors in language tasks, data-scarce or privacy-sensitive scenarios, and automated student design. This paper synthesizes empirical practices, mechanisms, theoretical insights, and practical guidance from recent studies to orient research and engineering choices for KD-based compression.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context‑Dependent Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When paired with complementary compression methods and task‑aware design choices, KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of a teacher model’s performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data‑free scenarios), and explicit treatment of robustness, rare‑token behaviors, and privacy. I argue that KD should be treated as a core engineering strategy whose full value is realized only when adapted to context through careful signal selection, data strategies, and architecture co‑design.

papers_seen.author: Hunter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints. Across vision and language tasks KD methods—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature and relational alignment—consistently enable substantial reductions in compute and memory while recovering much of teacher accuracy when applied with attention to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization dynamics. Practical KD pipelines typically combine distilled signals with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adopt data-aware strategies (augmentation, synthetic-data generation, or data-free protocols) to address real-world deployment challenges. Key open problems include robustly preserving long-tail or rare behaviors, handling distribution shift and privacy constraints, and automating student design for strict resource budgets.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost while attempting to preserve predictive performance. KD encompasses a range of mechanisms — soft-target (logit) matching, feature and intermediate-layer imitation, attention- or channel-based guidance, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, self-distillation, and data- or device-aware variants — and is applied across modalities including vision and language. Empirical work shows KD can yield substantial reductions in parameters and latency with modest accuracy loss, and in some settings can improve student generalization. Practical deployment couples KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and requires careful design choices around teacher-student alignment, data availability, and task-specific objectives.

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD encompasses soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and projector-based transforms, online and multi-teacher schedules, and data- or privacy-aware variants. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search) and careful teacher–student design, KD routinely yields substantial inference and memory savings while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical application requires attention to teacher quality, data availability, capacity and architecture mismatch, and task-specific objectives (e.g., robustness or privacy); addressing these issues motivates specialized distillation losses, student-aware teacher training, data synthesis, and adversarial or privacy-preserving protocols.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students for deployment in constrained environments. KD can transfer predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and structural inductive biases; it supports multi-teacher, progressive, adversarial, and data-constrained variants; and it can be combined with architecture-aware design and data strategies to improve efficiency, robustness, and domain adaptability. While highly effective in practice, KD's success depends on choices about what to transfer, how teachers and students are aligned, and the availability and suitability of data, so it should be treated as a flexible toolkit rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: The Pragmatic Power and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured into a practical toolkit for shrinking models, transferring behavior across architectures and modalities, and enabling deployment under compute, memory, or privacy constraints. Beyond straightforward teacher-to-student compression, distillation techniques combine with data augmentation, synthetic-data generation, and regularization to address limited data, cross-domain gaps, and interpretability needs. However, outcomes depend on choices about teacher quality, training data availability, and objective design; careful method selection is required to realize reliable, production-ready gains.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Favoring Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical, versatile pathway to produce compact models that preserve much of the performance of larger teachers while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When treated as a design paradigm—choosing what form of knowledge to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression primitives—KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade‑offs across modalities. KD should be adopted as the default first‑line compression method in deep learning and NLP while being applied with careful safeguards for data, robustness, and task alignment.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Practical, but Not a Panacea
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are essential tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. A wide family of methods — from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature transfer, projector-based alignment, data-free synthesis, and combinations with pruning or architecture search — let practitioners trade compute and memory for modest accuracy loss. However, KD’s effectiveness depends on optimization, data alignment, and the choice of distilled signals; it can replicate undesirable teacher behaviors and fails when teacher–student mismatch or data constraints are not addressed. Practical deployment therefore requires selecting KD variants that match application constraints and combining distillation with complementary compression and robustness techniques.

papers_seen.author: Short
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First-Line, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully—selecting appropriate distilled signals, co-designing teacher and student architectures, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods and data strategies—KD routinely achieves strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs in vision and language tasks. However, its success is context-dependent and requires explicit attention to data availability, teacher quality, robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Fernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural networks into smaller, more efficient models by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. A spectrum of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational patterns) and training regimes (offline teacher-to-student, online co-distillation, multi-teacher schedules, and data-free synthesis) enables practical trade-offs between performance, latency, and memory. Effective compression usually combines distillation with architecture-aware choices and complementary techniques such as pruning and quantization. Success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, and data availability; remaining challenges include distribution shift, preserving rare-token and domain-specific behavior, privacy-aware distillation, and reducing the computational cost of distillation itself.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Path to Compact, High-Quality Models in NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models for deployment. Across NLP and other modalities, distillation enables lightweight architectures to retain much of a teacher's performance while supporting additional compression techniques (pruning, quantization) and privacy-respecting or data-free workflows. However, distillation outcomes depend strongly on teacher–student compatibility, the form of distilled knowledge (logits, features, attention), access to data, and optimization choices. Best results arise when distillation is integrated with appropriate pre-training, architectural adapters (projectors or attention alignment), and, when necessary, data synthesis or domain adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Haynes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, general-purpose approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. When applied with attention to what knowledge is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), to teacher–student capacity alignment, and to data constraints, KD routinely yields substantial improvements in inference latency and memory while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: it carries risks (transfer of bias, privacy leakage, reduced robustness on distribution shift and rare tokens) and requires complementary techniques (task-aware objectives, architecture design, dataset strategies, and robustness/privacy safeguards) to be reliable in production. I argue KD should be treated as the first‑line, default strategy for model compression in deep learning and NLP, used proactively alongside targeted mitigations for its limits and with careful empirical validation.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD has proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling multimodal generation, compact evaluation metrics, and efficient inference. However, KD is not a black-box cure: its success depends on what is transferred (logits, features, intermediate layers), how teachers and students are paired or trained, and on optimization and regularization choices. I argue that KD should be viewed as a flexible toolkit—comprising feature-level mimicking, layer-aware projection, self- and teacher-free variants, and teacher-adaptation strategies—applied with careful attention to teacher-student interaction and training dynamics to achieve reliable compression in practice.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First-Line, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and empirically validated approach for converting large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Treated as a toolkit rather than a single loss, KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), training regimes (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free), and integration with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design). I argue KD should serve as the first-line strategy for model compression in modern deep learning and NLP pipelines, provided practitioners adopt principled, context-aware distillation recipes and pair KD with targeted validation for robustness and distributional concerns.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the central, practical toolkit for compressing large deep models into deployable students in both deep learning and NLP. KD provides flexible supervision (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, ensemble signals) and interoperates with complementary techniques (architecture search, pruning, quantization, data synthesis). When used systematically—selecting what to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity, leveraging data-aware or data-free strategies, and integrating KD into broader compression pipelines—KD enables strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployments. At the same time, careful attention to teacher quality, rare-token preservation, robustness, and domain shift is required to avoid predictable failure modes and to maximize real-world utility.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques that transfer knowledge from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining much of the teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels — softened output distributions, intermediate feature or attention imitation, and relational or layer-wise alignment — and composes naturally with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD yields substantial gains in latency, memory, and energy for deployed systems, but its success depends on careful design choices related to what is distilled, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability, and robustness or fairness requirements. Practical deployment treats KD as a core element of a hybrid compression pipeline, with task-aware signal selection, student-aware teacher design, and targeted remedies for distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, adversarial vulnerability, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become practical tools to reduce model size and computation while retaining much of the performance of large teachers. Across vision, speech, and natural language tasks, approaches include transferring soft logits, mimicking internal features or attention maps, layering/structural adaptations, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-preserving methods. Empirical results demonstrate that careful distillation can yield compact students that approach teacher accuracy and enable deployment in resource-constrained settings, but open challenges remain in robustness, task-specific distillation design, and distributed training dynamics.

papers_seen.author: Weber
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling substantial reductions in model size, latency, and memory while often preserving predictive performance. Modern KD extends beyond soft-target (logit) matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, contrastive and relational signals, online or teacher-free co-training, and privacy- or communication-aware protocols. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data availability; remaining challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, and reliable distillation when original data are limited or private.

papers_seen.author: Gross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD operates at multiple levels (softened output distributions, intermediate features and attention maps, relational/contrastive objectives, and module-level behavior), and is commonly combined with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (data-free synthesis, public transfer sets, augmentation). Empirical work shows well-designed KD pipelines often produce compact models that approach teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and careful choice of distillation signals. Open problems include aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or domain-specific behaviors, ensuring robustness under distribution shift, and developing principled teacher design and data-limited protocols.

papers_seen.author: Merritt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully — choosing what to transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps), aligning teacher and student capacity, and addressing data constraints — KD enables strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of appropriate data, and explicit safeguards for robustness and fairness. Combining KD with complementary techniques (architecture search, pruning, quantization, data augmentation, and privacy-aware protocols) and adopting task-adaptive distillation pipelines yields the most reliable real-world outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compacts large teacher models into smaller, faster students by transferring information beyond hard labels. A spectrum of KD strategies has been developed—soft-target (logit) transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, many-to-many layer mapping, multi-teacher and progressive schedules, self-distillation, and data-free variants—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows well-designed distillation pipelines can recover much of a teacher’s performance while delivering large gains in latency and memory, but outcomes depend on the choice of distillation signal, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints such as domain shift and privacy. Current practical directions emphasize representation-aware objectives, layer-alignment techniques, and hybrid pipelines that treat KD as a core element of system-level compression.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment in constrained environments. Advances across task-adaptive compression, data-free and zero-shot distillation, multi-teacher and meta-learned teaching, and self-distillation demonstrate KD's broad applicability. However, KD is not a panacea: success depends on data availability, the teacher–student optimization dynamics, and explicit design choices around architecture and training signals. Combining pre-training of compact models, task-aware architecture search, and sophisticated distillation protocols yields the best trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used and flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has grown from matching softened output distributions to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-representation matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, data-free/zero-shot synthesis, and architecture-aware co-design. Empirical work demonstrates KD's ability to reduce parameter counts and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance across vision, speech, and language tasks; its practical success depends on careful choices of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to manage data and augmentation. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under domain shift, preserving rare-token behavior in language models, privacy-sensitive settings, and principled combination of KD with other compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.
