papers_seen.author: Carrillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A broad family of KD techniques—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, using multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and synthesizing data when originals are unavailable—has proven effective across vision, language, and other modalities. Practical success depends on co-designing what is transferred, student architecture and capacity, and data strategies; important open problems include robust transfer under domain shift, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behaviors, data-free and privacy-sensitive distillation, and principled combinations of KD with other compression primitives.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: A Practical Case for Richer Knowledge Distillation in NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a necessary and practical tool for compressing large models and enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings, but its value depends critically on what is distilled and how. Soft-label matching transfers useful "dark knowledge" from ensembles, yet by itself often fails to capture internal structure, handle domain or data heterogeneity, or operate when original data are unavailable. Combining soft labels with internal- and feature-level guidance, architecture- and task-aware compression, and data- or privacy-aware generation strategies yields more robust, compact models that retain teacher performance across NLP and broader deep learning tasks.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are a widely adopted toolkit for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy of larger teachers. Research across vision and language characterizes KD as a family of methods—transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, relational structure, or training signals via specialized curricula or online exchanges—and shows that KD integrates naturally with pretraining, architecture design, and deployment-aware strategies. Practical success depends on matching the choice of knowledge (what to transfer), the teacher-student pairing (capacity and architecture), available data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and optimization curricula to the target task and constraints. While KD routinely yields substantial runtime and memory gains with modest accuracy loss, open challenges remain in handling domain shift, rare-token transfer in NLP, optimization mismatch, and large-scale or privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teachers' performance. Modern KD extends beyond soft-label matching to include representation-level objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, data-free or zero-shot variants, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search. KD has been applied successfully across domains — including language generation, ranking, detection, and federated settings — but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to manage data, privacy, and distributional shift. Practical deployment requires selecting distillation signals and training regimes that match student capacity and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features/attention, relational or structural signals) and can be applied in offline, online, ensemble, or data-constrained settings. Empirical results across vision, speech, and language show that appropriately designed distillation pipelines can deliver large efficiency gains with modest loss (and sometimes gains) in accuracy, but success depends on choices about what is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical deployments typically combine KD with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and require design attention to robustness, domain shift, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Webster
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal information from teacher models. A rich toolbox has emerged—ranging from softened-output matching to intermediate representation alignment, multi-teacher schedules, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and combinations with structural compression—that makes it possible to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints across vision and language tasks. Practical deployment requires attention to teacher–student compatibility, choice of distilled signals, data availability, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare-token and domain-specific behavior, and principled handling of teacher–student mismatch in heterogeneous settings.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller ones to reduce inference cost, improve deployability, or impart desirable properties (robustness, fairness, interpretability). Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, ensemble consensus, attention maps) and in what data is available (original training data, synthetic data, or no data). Practical systems combine KD with architecture-level compression (pruning, structured sparsity) and with training-time strategies (online or continual distillation, curriculum schedules) to trade off efficiency and accuracy. While KD yields strong empirical results across NLP, speech, vision, and generative models, open challenges remain in data-free settings, cross-domain generalization, preserving fairness and interpretability, and designing distillation objectives that best capture the teacher’s knowledge for a given task.

papers_seen.author: Benson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a reliable and versatile technique for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when combined with architecture-aware design, layer- and representation-level alignment, and appropriate data strategies. However, its success depends on careful choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle distributional or data-availability gaps; KD therefore belongs at the center of compression pipelines rather than as a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Practical Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, faster models suitable for production and edge deployment. Different KD variants—data-free, multi-teacher, online, feature-level, adversarial, and task-specific strategies—address practical constraints like lack of original data, communication or privacy limits, and the need to preserve representational quality. However, KD is not a panacea: its benefits depend on teacher-student capacity, dataset complexity, optimization choices, and the design of distillation signals. A pragmatic approach selects KD variants that match the application constraints and explicitly addresses optimization and data-complexity issues to maximize student performance while preserving efficiency and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying deep models in constrained environments. Work in this area spans simple teacher–student soft-label transfer to advanced feature- and layer-level matching, adversarial and data-free approaches, and automated search guided by distillation. Applications include compressing pre-trained language models, accelerating non-autoregressive translation, compressing generative models, and improving low-precision inference. Empirical and theoretical studies highlight both practical recipes (mixing hard and soft labels, many-to-many layer mappings, feature mimicking) and conceptual explanations (connections to label smoothing and regularization), while open challenges remain in retaining rare-token behavior, mitigating bias transfer, and scaling distillation to privacy- or data-limited settings.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to reproduce useful behavior of larger teacher models so that deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints becomes practical. KD encompasses a family of techniques — from matching teacher output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure — and is commonly combined with complementary compressions such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows that, when matched to student capacity and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Practical success depends on choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data access (including data-free alternatives), and robustness or fairness requirements; remaining challenges concern principled objective design, optimization under capacity mismatch, and reliable transfer of robustness and rare-token/long-tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression: Capability, Mechanisms, and Bounded Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach for converting large, high‑performance models into compact students that meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints. When designers choose appropriate distilled signals, align teacher and student capacities, and combine KD with complementary compression methods and data strategies, KD yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks. However, KD is not a universal solution: its benefits depend on teacher quality and compatibility, data availability, and explicit handling of robustness, long‑tail behaviors, and deployment constraints. This paper argues that KD should serve as a practical core of compression pipelines while being applied judiciously and in combination with other techniques to address known limits.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Effective Practices for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques reliably reduce large pretrained models to compact, efficient students suitable for deployment while preserving most of the teacher performance. Across NLP and multimodal tasks, practical compression requires strategies that (1) align representations at multiple levels, (2) focus on task-relevant information, and (3) handle limited or no access to original training data. Combining architecture-aware search, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, and improved input-side strategies (including data augmentation or data-free sample generation) yields compact models with strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs suitable for real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When combined with complementary practices—such as pretraining compact students, representation-level matching, curriculum scheduling, teacher ensembles, and data augmentation—KD yields strong tradeoffs between efficiency and performance across modalities and tasks. However, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data or domain mismatch; KD therefore functions best as a central, flexible component within a broader compression pipeline rather than as a one-size-fits-all cure.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical, flexible route to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. KD spans multiple mechanisms — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation transfer, layer-wise or progressive replacement, privacy- and data-aware variants — and can be combined with structural compression such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is highly effective in many realistic settings but is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, what form of knowledge is transferred, data availability (including few-shot or privacy-constrained scenarios), and careful optimization and evaluation. Viewed as a central yet context-sensitive tool, KD should be a default component of compression pipelines, applied in concert with complementary methods and guarded by targeted diagnostics for robustness and rare-token or out-of-distribution behavior.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Principled Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' predictive power. KD is most effective when it goes beyond naïve soft-label copying: matching internal representations, aligning inputs and tokenization, choosing appropriate data or synthesis strategies, and adapting teacher updates or curricula all materially affect transfer quality. KD should be used as part of a broader compression pipeline (architecture design, quantization, pruning, or data strategies) and with explicit checks for rare-token behavior, fairness, and robustness. When applied with these considerations, KD reliably produces compact models suitable for production constraints in vision, language, and other modalities.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Solis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from one or more high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple softened-logit matching into a diverse toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relation-aware losses, layer-mapping strategies for large pretrained transformers, self-distillation, curriculum-driven distillation, and complementary use with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs and enables deployment under stringent latency, memory, and privacy constraints, its success depends on careful selection of distilled signals, teacher–student co-design, data strategies, and mitigation of optimization, robustness, and distribution-shift failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Unifying Tool: Compression, Transfer, and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) began as a model compression technique but has evolved into a flexible framework that accomplishes compression, regularization, domain adaptation, continual learning, fairness mitigation, and inductive-bias transfer across architectures and modalities. By choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations, or module behavior) and how to weight multi-source supervision, practitioners can adapt KD to the constraints and objectives of specific tasks. This paper argues that KD should be treated not merely as a compression trick but as a general-purpose mechanism for shaping student models, and it synthesizes empirical and theoretical evidence to recommend practical best practices for applying KD across modern deep learning and NLP settings.

papers_seen.author: Dixon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from teachers. KD spans simple soft-target matching to richer schemes that mimic intermediate representations, attention, or relational signals, and it can be combined with pretraining, data augmentation, multi-teacher schedules, and architecture search. Practical effectiveness depends on aligning teacher signals to student capacity, managing limited or private data, and choosing inputs and objectives that preserve fine-grained behaviors. The following synthesis summarizes prevailing mechanisms, representative techniques, empirical strengths and failure modes, and practical recommendations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the System-Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated as a central, system-level approach to model compression and adaptation. By transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, or relational structure from larger teachers to smaller students, KD enables compact models that meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints while preserving much of teacher performance. Real-world success depends on co-designing teacher and student, selecting what signals to transfer, combining distillation with complementary compression techniques, and using data strategies (including data-free or few-shot protocols) to handle privacy- or data-limited settings. When applied thoughtfully, KD serves as a unifying, practical toolkit for creating efficient, deployable models across modalities; however, careful mitigation of teacher-induced biases, distribution shift, and robustness issues is required.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

Soft-label matching transfers useful "dark knowledge" from ensembles, yet by itself often fails to capture internal structure, handle domain or data heterogeneity, or operate when original data are unavailable. Combining soft labels with internal- and feature-level guidance, architecture- and task-aware compression, and data- or privacy-aware generation strategies yields more robust, compact models that retain teacher performance across NLP and broader deep learning tasks.'}, {'author': 'Perez', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are a widely adopted toolkit for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy of larger teachers. Research across vision and language characterizes KD as a family of methods—transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, relational structure, or training signals via specialized curricula or online exchanges—and shows that KD integrates naturally with pretraining, architecture design, and deployment-aware strategies. Practical success depends on matching the choice of knowledge (what to transfer), the teacher-student pairing (capacity and architecture), available data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and optimization curricula to the target task and constraints. While KD routinely yields substantial runtime and memory gains with modest accuracy loss, open challenges remain in handling domain shift, rare-token transfer in NLP, optimization mismatch, and large-scale or privacy-sensitive deployments.'}, {'author': 'Jackson', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teachers' performance. KD has been applied successfully across domains — including language generation, ranking, detection, and federated settings — but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to manage data, privacy, and distributional shift. Practical deployment requires selecting distillation signals and training regimes that match student capacity and deployment constraints."}, {'author': 'Beck', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features/attention, relational or structural signals) and can be applied in offline, online, ensemble, or data-constrained settings. Empirical results across vision, speech, and language show that appropriately designed distillation pipelines can deliver large efficiency gains with modest loss (and sometimes gains) in accuracy, but success depends on choices about what is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical deployments typically combine KD with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and require design attention to robustness, domain shift, and privacy.'}, {'author': 'Hill', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft', 'abstract': 'We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.'}, {'author': 'Hernandez', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.'}, {'author': 'Ramirez', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets', 'abstract': "The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch."}, {'author': 'Webster', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal information from teacher models. A rich toolbox has emerged—ranging from softened-output matching to intermediate representation alignment, multi-teacher schedules, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and combinations with structural compression—that makes it possible to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints across vision and language tasks. Practical deployment requires attention to teacher–student compatibility, choice of distilled signals, data availability, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare-token and domain-specific behavior, and principled handling of teacher–student mismatch in heterogeneous settings.'}, {'author': 'Hawkins', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition', 'abstract': 'While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.'}, {'author': 'Johnson', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller ones to reduce inference cost, improve deployability, or impart desirable properties (robustness, fairness, interpretability). Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, ensemble consensus, attention maps) and in what data is available (original training data, synthetic data, or no data). Practical systems combine KD with architecture-level compression (pruning, structured sparsity) and with training-time strategies (online or continual distillation, curriculum schedules) to trade off efficiency and accuracy. While KD yields strong empirical results across NLP, speech, vision, and generative models, open challenges remain in data-free settings, cross-domain generalization, preserving fairness and interpretability, and designing distillation objectives that best capture the teacher’s knowledge for a given task.'}, {'author': 'Benson', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a reliable and versatile technique for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when combined with architecture-aware design, layer- and representation-level alignment, and appropriate data strategies. However, its success depends on careful choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle distributional or data-availability gaps; KD therefore belongs at the center of compression pipelines rather than as a standalone silver bullet.'}, {'author': 'Mcclain', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Practical Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, faster models suitable for production and edge deployment. Different KD variants—data-free, multi-teacher, online, feature-level, adversarial, and task-specific strategies—address practical constraints like lack of original data, communication or privacy limits, and the need to preserve representational quality. However, KD is not a panacea: its benefits depend on teacher-student capacity, dataset complexity, optimization choices, and the design of distillation signals. A pragmatic approach selects KD variants that match the application constraints and explicitly addresses optimization and data-complexity issues to maximize student performance while preserving efficiency and privacy.'}, {'author': 'Williams', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation', 'abstract': 'Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.'}, {'author': 'Baker', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying deep models in constrained environments. Work in this area spans simple teacher–student soft-label transfer to advanced feature- and layer-level matching, adversarial and data-free approaches, and automated search guided by distillation. Applications include compressing pre-trained language models, accelerating non-autoregressive translation, compressing generative models, and improving low-precision inference. Empirical and theoretical studies highlight both practical recipes (mixing hard and soft labels, many-to-many layer mappings, feature mimicking) and conceptual explanations (connections to label smoothing and regularization), while open challenges remain in retaining rare-token behavior, mitigating bias transfer, and scaling distillation to privacy- or data-limited settings.'}, {'author': 'Munoz', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.'}, {'author': 'Herrera', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to reproduce useful behavior of larger teacher models so that deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints becomes practical. KD encompasses a family of techniques — from matching teacher output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure — and is commonly combined with complementary compressions such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search.
